0.title: Nehemiah: The God Who Remembers
0.overview:
The book of Nehemiah opens with a question. A Jewish official in the Persian palace at Susa, the king's cupbearer, asks some travellers from Judah how things are in Jerusalem, and hears that the survivors are in great trouble and shame and the wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates are destroyed by fire (1:3). He sits down and weeps, and prays for four months before he says a word to the king. The book that records a wall built in fifty-two days begins with a man on his knees.

In the Hebrew Bible Ezra and Nehemiah are one book. Nehemiah arrives in 445 BC, thirteen years after Ezra, with the king's letters and a troop of cavalry, and the story falls into three parts. Chapters 1-7: the wall, built against mockery, threats, a debt crisis inside the community and plots against Nehemiah himself, and finished with the help of our God (6:16). Chapters 8-10: the law read from dawn to noon at the Water Gate, the people weeping and then told that the joy of the LORD is your strength (8:10), the great prayer that tells Israel's whole history as the history of a God who did not forsake them (9:17-31), and a covenant signed and sealed. Chapters 11-13: the empty city peopled, the wall dedicated with two choirs walking along the top of it until the joy of Jerusalem was heard far away (12:43) — and then Nehemiah comes back from the Persian court to find almost every promise of the covenant broken.

Much of the book is Nehemiah's own memoir, in the first person, and he is one of the most vivid men in the Bible: afraid before the king and going in anyway, praying in the three seconds between a question and an answer (2:4), refusing his governor's allowance for twelve years, sleeping in his clothes on the wall, throwing an enemy's furniture into a temple courtyard. And all through it he prays one prayer: remember. He begins by asking God to remember the word he gave Moses (1:8), and his last words are Remember me, O my God, for good (13:31).

The book is honest in a way that repays close reading. It copies out the register of the first return, whose figures do not add up to its own total, and lets them stand. It reports that a man who built two sections of the wall had married his daughter into the enemy's family (6:18), and that the high priest's grandson married Sanballat's daughter (13:28). It ends not with the triumph of chapter 12 but with a governor putting the same reforms in place a second time. Several of the lists in this commentary are treated by what they mean rather than name by name; the chapters the book turns on — the prayer of chapter 1, the reading of chapter 8, the prayer of chapter 9 — are treated at length.

And the book points beyond itself at almost every turn. Nehemiah confesses his people's sins as we, and one Intercessor took on sins that were not his (2 Cor 5:21). His enemies accused him of letting prophets proclaim There is a king in Judah (6:7); it was false of him and true of the King Zechariah had promised (Zech 9:9), who died under the charge the King of the Jews. The joy of the Feast of Booths was waiting for the day when Jesus stood up and cried out, If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37). The covenant the people signed could not change a heart, and the book leaves us waiting for the one that does: I will write it on their hearts (Jer 31:33).

Its closing chapter is the latest history the Old Testament tells, and its last word is a prayer. Four and a half centuries later, outside the walls of the same city, a dying man prayed almost the same words — Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom — and was answered at once: today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:42-43). The God of Nehemiah is the God who remembers.

1.title: The Man Who Wept for a City
1.text: <sup>1</sup>The words of Nehemiah the son of Hacaliah. Now it happened in the month of Chislev, in the twentieth year, as I was in Susa the citadel,<sup>2</sup>that Hanani, one of my brothers, came with certain men from Judah. And I asked them concerning the Jews who escaped, who had survived the exile, and concerning Jerusalem.<sup>3</sup>And they said to me, "The remnant there in the province who had survived the exile is in great trouble and shame. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates are destroyed by fire."<sup>4</sup>As soon as I heard these words I sat down and wept and mourned for days, and I continued fasting and praying before the God of heaven.<sup>5</sup>And I said, "O LORD God of heaven, the great and awesome God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments,<sup>6</sup>let your ear be attentive and your eyes open, to hear the prayer of your servant that I now pray before you day and night for the people of Israel your servants, confessing the sins of the people of Israel, which we have sinned against you. Even I and my father's house have sinned.<sup>7</sup>We have acted very corruptly against you and have not kept the commandments, the statutes, and the rules that you commanded your servant Moses.<sup>8</sup>Remember the word that you commanded your servant Moses, saying, 'If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you among the peoples,<sup>9</sup>but if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, though your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen, to make my name dwell there.'<sup>10</sup>They are your servants and your people, whom you have redeemed by your great power and by your strong hand.<sup>11</sup>O Lord, let your ear be attentive to the prayer of your servant, and to the prayer of your servants who delight to fear your name, and give success to your servant today, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man." Now I was cupbearer to the king.
1.overview: In Chislev of Artaxerxes' twentieth year (about 445 BC), Nehemiah, a Jew serving in the Persian palace at Susa, asks his brother Hanani about Jerusalem and hears that the survivors are in great trouble and shame and the wall is broken down, its gates burned (vv. 1-3) — perhaps the old ruin of 586 BC, perhaps the fresh wreck of the attempt Artaxerxes himself had stopped (Ezra 4:21-23). He sits down and weeps, and fasts and prays for four months (v. 4; cf. 2:1). The prayer (vv. 5-11) is built almost entirely from Scripture: Daniel's address to the great and awesome God who keeps covenant and steadfast love, Solomon's plea to be heard, a confession that includes I and my father's house, Moses' warning and promise of scattering and gathering, and Moses' own argument after the golden calf: they are your servants and your people, whom you have redeemed. It ends with a request for mercy in the sight of this man, and only then tells us who is praying: Now I was cupbearer to the king.
1.theology:
Nehemiah prays God's own words back to him. The threat of scattering had been kept to the letter; therefore the promise of gathering will be kept too. That is the ground of all confident prayer: not the strength of our feeling, but the fact that God has spoken and does not go back on his word.

He confesses as we and pleads that the people are God's by redemption. Both movements point beyond him. The true Intercessor took on sins that were not his (2 Cor 5:21), pleads for a people bought with his own blood (1 Pet 1:18-19), and stands not as a trembling cupbearer before a Persian king but at the right hand of the Father, where he always lives to make intercession for them (Heb 7:25).
1.examples:
Nehemiah's first act in his own book is to ask how God's people are.

Susa the citadel is Esther's address; God had put his people in that palace before.

He prayed for four months before he said a word to the king.

His opening sentence is Daniel's, prayed over the same ruins ninety-four years earlier.

He was born in exile, and he still said I and my father's house have sinned.

The king he prayed about had signed the order stopping the wall, until a decree is made by me.

We learn he is the king's cupbearer only after he has finished praying.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Wall of Jerusalem Is Broken Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the month of Chislev, in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, Nehemiah is in Susa the citadel when his brother Hanani arrives from Judah (vv. 1-2). He asks about the survivors and about Jerusalem, and the answer is bad on both counts: The remnant there in the province who had survived the exile is in great trouble and shame. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates are destroyed by fire (v. 3). As soon as I heard these words I sat down and wept and mourned for days, and I continued fasting and praying before the God of heaven (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The book that will record a wall built in fifty-two days opens with a man who does nothing for four months but pray. That order is not incidental to the building; it is the foundation of it. Nehemiah will plan brilliantly, but he will never plan first.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus also wept over Jerusalem, and for the opposite reason: Nehemiah wept because its walls were down, and Jesus wept because he knew they would come down again: they will not leave one stone upon another (Luke 19:41-44).

verseByVerse.quote: The words of Nehemiah the son of Hacaliah. Now it happened in the month of Chislev, in the twentieth year, as I was in Susa the citadel, that Hanani, one of my brothers, came with certain men from Judah. And I asked them concerning the Jews who escaped, who had survived the exile, and concerning Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words of Nehemiah the son of Hacaliah. What follows is, for most of its length, a memoir written in the first person — I asked, I sat down, I was cupbearer. We are hearing the man himself.

The date is the month of Chislev, November into December, in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes I, about 445 BC. The place is Susa the citadel, the winter palace of the Persian kings. It is the same address as the book of Esther (Esth 1:2), where a Jewish girl had become queen a generation earlier under this king's father. God's people had friends in that palace before, and he had put them there.

Nehemiah was very likely born in exile and had never seen Jerusalem. He had a post at the centre of the most powerful court on earth, and no personal need of that ruined city at all. Then his brother Hanani (he calls him my brother Hanani again at 7:2) arrives with men from Judah, and the first thing Nehemiah does in his own book is ask a question. I asked them concerning the Jews who escaped, who had survived the exile, and concerning Jerusalem.

He asked about the people first and the place second. And he asked at all. A comfortable man can go a long time without asking how things are with the people of God, because the answer might cost him something. Nehemiah wanted to know.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to me, "The remnant there in the province who had survived the exile is in great trouble and shame. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates are destroyed by fire."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The remnant there in the province who had survived the exile is in great trouble and shame. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates are destroyed by fire.

Picture what that meant. An ancient city without a wall was hardly a city. Anyone could walk in at night. Traders would not risk their goods there, and nobody of means would live there. The gates were charcoal lying in the gateways. The temple stood on its hill, rebuilt seventy years before, in the middle of a settlement that could not shut a door.

Which ruin is meant is not certain. The walls had been down since the Babylonians burned the city in 586 BC, and some think Hanani is describing that old desolation. But Ezra 4 records that under this same Artaxerxes the Jews began rebuilding the walls, their neighbours wrote to the king, and he ordered the work stopped; his officials went in haste to the Jews at Jerusalem and by force and power made them cease (Ezra 4:23). A fresh wreck, a wall pulled down again after the people had dared to start it, fits a man who sits down and weeps for days far better than a fact everyone had known for a century and a half.

And the word shame will not leave this book. It is the derision Nehemiah means to end at 2:17, the taunt of 4:4, the taunts of the nations at 5:9. The wall is stone and mortar, but it is built against a word: the sneer of neighbours who looked at the ruin and said that the God of Israel could not look after his own.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as I heard these words I sat down and wept and mourned for days, and I continued fasting and praying before the God of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As soon as I heard these words I sat down and wept and mourned for days, and I continued fasting and praying before the God of heaven.

He sat down. The legs went. Then days of weeping and mourning, and then, continuing, fasting and prayer. How long is shown by the next date in the book: this is Chislev, and Nehemiah speaks to the king in Nisan (2:1). Four months. The man who will get a wall built in fifty-two days spends more than twice that long on his knees before he lays a stone.

The God of heaven is the title Cyrus used in his decree (Ezra 1:2), the name of God as he stood over an empire. Nehemiah is praying from inside the court of the King of kings of Persia, to the God who reigns over the one he serves.

Here is a test. Nehemiah was safe, well fed and well placed, and the ruin was months of travel away. It cost him four months of grief because it was God's city and God's people, and their shame was God's shame. What does the state of the church cost you — a congregation dwindling, a family that has walked away from the faith, a cause that has gone cold? Many readers already carry some grief of that kind. Nehemiah shows what to do with it. Do not bury it, and do not rush past it into a plan. Take it before the God of heaven, and keep taking it until he opens a door.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prayer opens with who God is: the great and awesome God who keeps covenant and steadfast love (v. 5). It asks him to listen, and confesses the nation's sin as Nehemiah's own: Even I and my father's house have sinned (vv. 6-7). It holds God to his word through Moses — scattered if unfaithful, gathered if they return (vv. 8-9). It pleads that they are his people, whom you have redeemed by your great power and by your strong hand (v. 10). And it asks for one thing: give success to your servant today, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man. Now I was cupbearer to the king (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Nearly every line of this prayer is borrowed. Its first sentence is Daniel's, its request to be heard is Solomon's, its promise is Moses' in Deuteronomy, and its plea for the people is the argument Moses used after the golden calf. Nehemiah prays in the language God has already used, which is why he can pray it with confidence.
verseByVerse.examples: The book begins with Nehemiah asking God to remember the word (v. 8) and ends with him asking God to remember me, O my God, for good (13:31). Everything between is a man working inside a promise and trusting God to keep the account.

verseByVerse.quote: And I said, "O LORD God of heaven, the great and awesome God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments,
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD God of heaven, the great and awesome God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments.

Before he says a word about Jerusalem, he says who God is. And the words are not his own. They are Daniel's, almost exactly: O Lord, the great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments (Dan 9:4). Daniel prayed that prayer in Babylon, about ninety-four years before, when he read in Jeremiah that the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years (Dan 9:2). Daniel was praying over the same ruins. God answered him with the decree of Cyrus. Now the temple was standing and the walls were not, and Nehemiah picks up Daniel's prayer where Daniel left it.

Daniel had it in turn from Moses (Deut 7:9). Covenant is the promise God has bound himself to; steadfast love, hesed, is the loyalty behind the promise, the love that keeps coming back. But notice what the sentence says: he keeps covenant with those who love him and keep his commandments. The next two verses will confess that Israel had not. The prayer's first sentence has already named the problem it has to solve.

verseByVerse.quote: let your ear be attentive and your eyes open, to hear the prayer of your servant that I now pray before you day and night for the people of Israel your servants, confessing the sins of the people of Israel, which we have sinned against you. Even I and my father's house have sinned. We have acted very corruptly against you and have not kept the commandments, the statutes, and the rules that you commanded your servant Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let your ear be attentive and your eyes open, to hear the prayer of your servant that I now pray before you day and night. This is Solomon's language at the dedication of the temple: let your eyes be open and your ears attentive to the prayer of this place (2 Chr 6:40), open night and day toward this house (1 Kgs 8:29). Solomon asked God to listen to prayers made toward that house when his people sinned. Nehemiah is making one.

Confessing the sins of the people of Israel, which we have sinned against you. Even I and my father's house have sinned. We have acted very corruptly against you and have not kept the commandments, the statutes, and the rules that you commanded your servant Moses.

Listen to the pronouns: the people of Israel, then we, then I and my father's house. He does not stand at a distance and describe the nation's failures to God. He puts himself and his family inside the guilt. He was born long after the exile began; he could have said they. He never does.

A question a reader can put to himself: when you pray about what is wrong in the church, is the subject of the sentence they or we? Nehemiah's we was honest, for he was a sinner himself, and his confession was shared guilt. There is one Intercessor who could have said they truthfully and still took the sin as though it were his: For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Cor 5:21).

verseByVerse.quote: Remember the word that you commanded your servant Moses, saying, 'If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you among the peoples, but if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, though your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen, to make my name dwell there.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember the word that you commanded your servant Moses, saying, If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you among the peoples, but if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, though your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen, to make my name dwell there.

This is not one verse of Moses but the gist of several, gathered up by a man who knew them well. Scatter you among the peoples is the warning of Leviticus 26:33 and Deuteronomy 4:27. Your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there is Deuteronomy 30:4, nearly word for word. The place that I have chosen, to make my name dwell there is Deuteronomy 12:11. Nehemiah is quoting the whole covenant back to the God who made it.

And look at the logic. The first half of that word had come true to the letter: they had been unfaithful, and they had been scattered, and Nehemiah is praying from Persia to prove it. So the second half is just as sure. The exile was the evidence that God keeps his word. A God who kept the threat will keep the promise.

Unfaithful is the word Leviticus uses for Israel's treachery, and Leviticus had said what should happen next: if they confess their iniquity and the iniquity of their fathers ... then I will remember my covenant (Lev 26:40-42). That is exactly the order of this prayer. Nehemiah has confessed, and now he asks God to remember. It is the first of many times the word appears in this book, and the book's last words are the same prayer turned on himself: Remember me, O my God, for good (13:31).

verseByVerse.quote: They are your servants and your people, whom you have redeemed by your great power and by your strong hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They are your servants and your people, whom you have redeemed by your great power and by your strong hand.

These are Moses' words on the worst day in Israel's history. After the golden calf, God said to Moses, Let me alone, that I may destroy them (Deut 9:14), and Moses lay on his face for forty days and argued: do not destroy your people and your heritage, whom you have redeemed through your greatness (Deut 9:26); they are your people and your heritage, whom you brought out by your great power (9:29).

The argument is not that the people deserved better. It is that they belong to God and that he paid for them. Redeemed means bought back. You do not throw away what cost you that much.

That argument is stronger now than when Moses and Nehemiah made it, because the price is greater. You were ransomed ... not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Pet 1:18-19). Whoever has been bought at that price has an Intercessor who can say to the Father, of the weakest of his people: they are yours, and look what they cost.

verseByVerse.quote: O Lord, let your ear be attentive to the prayer of your servant, and to the prayer of your servants who delight to fear your name, and give success to your servant today, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man." Now I was cupbearer to the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O Lord, let your ear be attentive to the prayer of your servant, and to the prayer of your servants who delight to fear your name. He is not alone. Somewhere others were praying the same prayer, people who took pleasure in reverence for God's name. He asks God to hear all of them together.

And give success to your servant today, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man. Today, because he has picked a day. This man, because the most powerful ruler on earth is, before God, a man.

And this particular man had put the problem there. Artaxerxes was the king who had ordered the building stopped, in a letter preserved in Ezra 4: make a decree that these men be made to cease, and that this city be not rebuilt, until a decree is made by me (Ezra 4:21). Until a decree is made by me. The king had left himself one door, and Nehemiah was praying to walk through it: to ask the emperor to reverse his own order. In Persia, a servant who displeased the king could lose his head. He knows what he is asking for.

Now I was cupbearer to the king. Only after the prayer do we learn who has been praying. The cupbearer handled what the king drank, a post given only to a man the king trusted with his life, and it meant that Nehemiah would stand within arm's length of the throne. That is the whole chapter in its last line: a man with a broken heart for God's city and access to the king.

We have a greater one. Nehemiah would go in trembling, afraid of the king's face (2:2). Our Intercessor sits at the right hand of the throne — we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses — so that we may with confidence draw near to the throne of grace (Heb 4:15-16); and he always lives to make intercession for us (Heb 7:25). The cupbearer had to wait four months for his moment. The Son never has to wait at all.

2.title: Vision in the Dark
2.text: <sup>1</sup>In the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, when wine was before him, I took up the wine and gave it to the king. Now I had not been sad in his presence.<sup>2</sup>And the king said to me, "Why is your face sad, seeing you are not sick? This is nothing but sadness of the heart." Then I was very much afraid.<sup>3</sup>I said to the king, "Let the king live forever! Why should not my face be sad, when the city, the place of my fathers' graves, lies in ruins, and its gates have been destroyed by fire?"<sup>4</sup>Then the king said to me, "What are you requesting?" So I prayed to the God of heaven.<sup>5</sup>And I said to the king, "If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor in your sight, that you send me to Judah, to the city of my fathers' graves, that I may rebuild it."<sup>6</sup>And the king said to me (the queen sitting beside him), "How long will you be gone, and when will you return?" So it pleased the king to send me when I had given him a time.<sup>7</sup>And I said to the king, "If it pleases the king, let letters be given me to the governors of the province Beyond the River, that they may let me pass through until I come to Judah,<sup>8</sup>and a letter to Asaph, the keeper of the king's forest, that he may give me timber to make beams for the gates of the fortress of the temple, and for the wall of the city, and for the house that I shall occupy." And the king granted me what I asked, for the good hand of my God was upon me.<sup>9</sup>Then I came to the governors of the province Beyond the River and gave them the king's letters. Now the king had sent with me officers of the army and horsemen.<sup>10</sup>But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant heard this, it displeased them greatly that someone had come to seek the welfare of the people of Israel.<sup>11</sup>So I went to Jerusalem and was there three days.<sup>12</sup>Then I arose in the night, I and a few men with me. And I told no one what my God had put into my heart to do for Jerusalem. There was no animal with me but the one on which I rode.<sup>13</sup>I went out by night by the Valley Gate to the Dragon Spring and to the Dung Gate, and I inspected the walls of Jerusalem that were broken down and its gates that had been destroyed by fire.<sup>14</sup>Then I went on to the Fountain Gate and to the King's Pool, but there was no room for the animal that was under me to pass.<sup>15</sup>Then I went up in the night by the valley and inspected the wall, and I turned back and entered by the Valley Gate, and so returned.<sup>16</sup>And the officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing, and I had not yet told the Jews, the priests, the nobles, the officials, and the rest who were to do the work.<sup>17</sup>Then I said to them, "You see the trouble we are in, how Jerusalem lies in ruins with its gates burned. Come, let us build the wall of Jerusalem, that we may no longer suffer derision."<sup>18</sup>And I told them of the hand of my God that had been upon me for good, and also of the words that the king had spoken to me. And they said, "Let us rise up and build." So they strengthened their hands for the good work.<sup>19</sup>But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant and Geshem the Arab heard of it, they jeered at us and despised us and said, "What is this thing that you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?"<sup>20</sup>Then I replied to them, "The God of heaven will make us prosper, and we his servants will arise and build, but you have no portion or right or claim in Jerusalem."
2.overview: Four months after the report, Nehemiah's grief shows on his face as he serves the king his wine. Why is your face sad? Terrified, he answers that the city of my fathers' graves lies in ruins, never naming Jerusalem to the king who had stopped its building (vv. 1-3). Asked what he wants, he prays in the moment and asks to be sent to rebuild it, with letters of passage and timber from the king's forest; the king grants it, for the good hand of my God was upon me — Ezra's own phrase (vv. 4-8). He travels with the cavalry escort Ezra had refused (v. 9), to the displeasure of Sanballat and Tobiah (v. 10). After three days he rides the ruins alone at night (vv. 11-16), then calls the leaders — Come, let us build the wall of Jerusalem — telling them of God's hand, and they answer Let us rise up and build (vv. 17-18). To the jeer Are you rebelling against the king? he replies that the God of heaven will prosper them, and the enemies have no portion or right or claim in Jerusalem (vv. 19-20).
2.theology:
God's providence works through a servant's sad face, a king's question, a three-second prayer, and a practical list of letters and timber. Prayer and planning are not rivals: the man who prayed four months also knew what beams he needed. And the good hand of God rests equally on Ezra, who refused an escort, and on Nehemiah, who accepted one; faith is not a method.

The builder who left a palace for a ruin is a real but limited likeness of Christ, who came without letters or horsemen (Phil 2:7), and who was accused of the same rebellion against the king (John 19:12).
2.examples:
He kept his grief off his face for four months, and then the king noticed.

He never said the word Jerusalem to the king.

He prayed in the three seconds between a question and an answer.

The timber for the gates came out of the king's pardes, his paradise.

Ezra refused a cavalry escort; Nehemiah took one; God's hand was on both.

On the east side the rubble was too thick for a donkey.

He had been in the city three days and said the trouble we are in.

His enemies will have no memorial in the city; he asks God to remember him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Good Hand of My God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Nisan, four months after the news, Nehemiah hands the king his wine with a face he can no longer control. Why is your face sad, seeing you are not sick? Then I was very much afraid (vv. 1-2). He answers that the city, the place of my fathers' graves, lies in ruins (v. 3). What are you requesting? So I prayed to the God of heaven (v. 4) — and asked to be sent to rebuild it (v. 5), named a time (v. 6), and asked for letters of safe passage and timber from the king's forest (vv. 7-8). And the king granted me what I asked, for the good hand of my God was upon me (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Four months of prayer, and then the answer came through a slip in a servant's composure that he had not planned and could not have staged. God turned the king's heart (Prov 21:1) by way of Nehemiah's sad face.

verseByVerse.quote: In the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, when wine was before him, I took up the wine and gave it to the king. Now I had not been sad in his presence. And the king said to me, "Why is your face sad, seeing you are not sick? This is nothing but sadness of the heart." Then I was very much afraid. I said to the king, "Let the king live forever! Why should not my face be sad, when the city, the place of my fathers' graves, lies in ruins, and its gates have been destroyed by fire?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, when wine was before him, I took up the wine and gave it to the king. Nisan is March into April. Chapter 1 was also dated to the twentieth year, in Chislev; Nehemiah evidently counts the king's years from the autumn, so the two dates are four months apart in the same regnal year.

Now I had not been sad in his presence. For four months he had carried the grief and kept it off his face. A Persian king did not care to see sorrow near him; in the book of Esther no one was allowed to enter the king's gate clothed in sackcloth (Esth 4:2). And then one day, with the cup in his hand, the mask slipped.

Why is your face sad, seeing you are not sick? This is nothing but sadness of the heart. Then I was very much afraid. The king had seen straight through him. An unhappy servant close to the royal cup could look like a dangerous one.

Nehemiah's own record says plainly that he was terrified. Courage in Scripture is not the absence of fear. It is doing the next right thing while afraid. A reader who is shaking at some conversation he knows he has to have is in good company here.

Let the king live forever! Why should not my face be sad, when the city, the place of my fathers' graves, lies in ruins, and its gates have been destroyed by fire? Notice what he does not say. He does not say Jerusalem. This king had once been told it was that rebellious and wicked city (Ezra 4:12) and had ordered its building stopped. So Nehemiah speaks of his fathers' graves, a claim any man in any nation would understand, and lets the king reach the name for himself. Truthful, and wise.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to me, "What are you requesting?" So I prayed to the God of heaven. And I said to the king, "If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor in your sight, that you send me to Judah, to the city of my fathers' graves, that I may rebuild it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the king said to me, What are you requesting? So I prayed to the God of heaven.

A king has asked a question and is waiting for the answer. There are perhaps three seconds before silence becomes insolence. Into those three seconds Nehemiah puts a prayer — no words spoken aloud, no bowed head the king would notice, a cry sent upward between the question and the answer.

That kind of prayer does not come from nowhere. The man who could pray in three seconds had been praying for four months. The long prayer made the short one possible; the habit made the reflex. Here is a question to put to yourself: in the pause before you answer a hard question at work, at home, on the telephone, is the God of heaven the first one you turn to? If not, the remedy is not a technique for that moment. It is the four months before it.

And I said to the king, If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor in your sight, that you send me to Judah, to the city of my fathers' graves, that I may rebuild it. The request is enormous. He is asking the king to send his own cupbearer to rebuild the city he had forbidden to be rebuilt. And he still has not named it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king said to me (the queen sitting beside him), "How long will you be gone, and when will you return?" So it pleased the king to send me when I had given him a time. And I said to the king, "If it pleases the king, let letters be given me to the governors of the province Beyond the River, that they may let me pass through until I come to Judah, and a letter to Asaph, the keeper of the king's forest, that he may give me timber to make beams for the gates of the fortress of the temple, and for the wall of the city, and for the house that I shall occupy." And the king granted me what I asked, for the good hand of my God was upon me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the king said to me (the queen sitting beside him), How long will you be gone, and when will you return? The queen is an eyewitness's detail; he remembered who was in the room. And the question is already a yes. The king is not asking whether, but when. Nehemiah named a time. In the end he governed Judah for twelve years (5:14) before returning to the king (13:6).

Then the petition turns practical: letters to the governors Beyond the River, the Persian province west of the Euphrates, for safe passage; and a letter to Asaph, the keeper of the king's forest, for timber — beams for the gates of the temple fortress, for the city wall, and for his own house. He had spent four months praying, and it turns out he had also spent them thinking. He knew what he needed down to the timber. Prayer and planning were never rivals in this man.

The word for the king's forest, pardes, is the Persian word for a royal park that has given us our word paradise. The timber for Jerusalem's gates came out of the king's paradise.

And the king granted me what I asked, for the good hand of my God was upon me. That is Ezra's sentence. Of Ezra it was written that the king granted him all that he asked, for the hand of the LORD his God was on him (Ezra 7:6), and the good hand of his God was on him (7:9). Thirteen years later the same hand rests on the second man. The king did the granting. God's hand is the reason he did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–20 — Let Us Rise Up and Build
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nehemiah travels with the king's letters and a cavalry escort, and of Sanballat and Tobiah we read that it displeased them greatly that someone had come to seek the welfare of the people of Israel (vv. 9-10). Three days in the city; then a night ride round the ruins with a few men, telling no one (vv. 11-16). Then: Come, let us build the wall of Jerusalem, that we may no longer suffer derision (v. 17). He tells them of God's hand and the king's words, and they answer Let us rise up and build (v. 18). The enemies jeer — Are you rebelling against the king? (v. 19) — and Nehemiah answers in God's name: you have no portion or right or claim in Jerusalem (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter's word is good: God's good hand (v. 8), the good of Israel that the enemy resents (v. 10), the hand upon him for good and the good work (v. 18). The book will end on it: Remember me, O my God, for good (13:31).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I came to the governors of the province Beyond the River and gave them the king's letters. Now the king had sent with me officers of the army and horsemen. But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant heard this, it displeased them greatly that someone had come to seek the welfare of the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I came to the governors of the province Beyond the River and gave them the king's letters. Now the king had sent with me officers of the army and horsemen.

Put that beside Ezra. Thirteen years earlier Ezra had made the same journey and would not ask for soldiers: I was ashamed to ask the king for a band of soldiers and horsemen to protect us against the enemy on our way (Ezra 8:22), because he had told the king that God protects those who seek him. Nehemiah rides in with cavalry. And both men are said to have had the good hand of God upon them.

So neither is a rule. There are times when faith refuses the means on offer, so that everyone will see that God did it, and times when faith accepts them with thanks, because God provided them. Ezra was travelling as a teacher of God's law, and Nehemiah as the king's governor. The same God was with the man who went without a guard and the man who went with one.

But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant heard this, it displeased them greatly that someone had come to seek the welfare of the people of Israel. Sanballat was governor of Samaria, to the north; Tobiah was an official in Ammon, across the Jordan, with friends inside Jerusalem (6:17-19). A weak Jerusalem suited them both. Their complaint is the most honest thing they say in the whole book: someone had come to do these people good.

verseByVerse.quote: So I went to Jerusalem and was there three days. Then I arose in the night, I and a few men with me. And I told no one what my God had put into my heart to do for Jerusalem. There was no animal with me but the one on which I rode. I went out by night by the Valley Gate to the Dragon Spring and to the Dung Gate, and I inspected the walls of Jerusalem that were broken down and its gates that had been destroyed by fire. Then I went on to the Fountain Gate and to the King's Pool, but there was no room for the animal that was under me to pass. Then I went up in the night by the valley and inspected the wall, and I turned back and entered by the Valley Gate, and so returned. And the officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing, and I had not yet told the Jews, the priests, the nobles, the officials, and the rest who were to do the work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I went to Jerusalem and was there three days. Ezra had done the same on arriving (Ezra 8:32). A man coming off a journey of months does not start a revolution on the first morning.

Then I arose in the night, I and a few men with me. And I told no one what my God had put into my heart to do for Jerusalem. The plan was God's, put into my heart, and he kept it to himself. Tobiah had friends in the city, and a plan announced before it is ready is a plan handed to the opposition.

Then comes the ride. Out by the Valley Gate on the west, down to the Dragon Spring and the Dung Gate at the southern tip of the city, round to the Fountain Gate and the King's Pool, and there no room for the animal that was under me to pass. On the steep eastern slope the stone of the old wall and the terraces had tumbled into the valley in heaps too choked for a donkey to pick through. So he went on foot, up in the night by the valley, looking at the wall from below, and came back in by the gate he had left by.

A man walking in the dark along a ruin, touching the burned timber, measuring the size of the problem alone before he asks anyone else to lift a stone. He would not call people to a work he had not seen with his own eyes. And the officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing — nobody yet, the Jews, the priests, the nobles, the officials, and the rest who were to do the work. He already calls them the ones who were to do the work.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said to them, "You see the trouble we are in, how Jerusalem lies in ruins with its gates burned. Come, let us build the wall of Jerusalem, that we may no longer suffer derision." And I told them of the hand of my God that had been upon me for good, and also of the words that the king had spoken to me. And they said, "Let us rise up and build." So they strengthened their hands for the good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I said to them, You see the trouble we are in, how Jerusalem lies in ruins with its gates burned. Come, let us build the wall of Jerusalem, that we may no longer suffer derision.

The trouble we are in. He had lived in the city three days. He could have said you. He said we, as he had said it in his prayer (1:6). And at last he names the city: Jerusalem, twice. Derision is the shame Hanani reported in 1:3: the neighbours' sneer, which a wall would silence.

And I told them of the hand of my God that had been upon me for good, and also of the words that the king had spoken to me. Testimony first. He did not begin with a plan or a rota. He told them what God had done — the prayer, the sad face, the question, the letters — and then what the king had said. The people of Jerusalem had watched the last attempt at a wall pulled down by force. What could make them try again was the news that God had moved.

And they said, Let us rise up and build. So they strengthened their hands for the good work. Count the good in this chapter: the good hand of God (v. 8), the good of Israel that the enemy resented (the welfare of v. 10 is the same word), the hand upon him for good, and now the good work. The enemy hated the good; God's hand was for it; the people put their hands to it. When Nehemiah's last recorded words are Remember me, O my God, for good (13:31), he is asking to be counted in with this.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant and Geshem the Arab heard of it, they jeered at us and despised us and said, "What is this thing that you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?" Then I replied to them, "The God of heaven will make us prosper, and we his servants will arise and build, but you have no portion or right or claim in Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant and Geshem the Arab heard of it, they jeered at us and despised us and said, What is this thing that you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?

Now there are three: Sanballat from Samaria to the north, Tobiah from Ammon to the east, Geshem the Arab from the desert to the south. Jerusalem is ringed. And their first weapon is a laugh, then the old charge: rebelling against the king. It had worked before; that was exactly the accusation in the letter that stopped the wall (Ezra 4:12-16). This time it was absurd, because the king's letters were in Nehemiah's baggage. But it is the charge the world reaches for whenever God's people build, and it was the charge that crucified the Son of God: Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar (John 19:12).

Then I replied to them, The God of heaven will make us prosper, and we his servants will arise and build, but you have no portion or right or claim in Jerusalem.

He had the king's letters and he did not wave them. He answered in God's name. The God of heaven will make us prosper; we are his servants. The last word, claim, is literally memorial, a remembrance. Sanballat and his friends will have no memorial in Jerusalem. The man who says so will end his book asking God to remember him.

Nehemiah left a palace and a king's favour to live among ruins and derision because he loved God's people. The likeness to Christ is real, and so is its limit. Nehemiah went with the king's letters and a troop of horsemen. The Son of God emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant (Phil 2:7), and came with neither, into a far greater ruin, to build a city whose enemies will have no memorial in it at all.
