3.overview: A register of the builders, section by section, beginning with Eliashib the high priest at the Sheep Gate (v. 1) and going anticlockwise round the whole city — north, west, south and up the eastern side — until the goldsmiths and merchants close the circuit back at the Sheep Gate (v. 32). Priests and Levites, men of Jericho, Gibeon and Tekoa, goldsmiths and perfumers, district rulers, temple servants and merchants all take a stretch; Shallum builds he and his daughters (v. 12); a ruler takes the Dung Gate (v. 14); several build opposite his own house; seven do another section. Only the nobles of Tekoa would not stoop to serve their Lord (v. 5), and their townsmen did two sections. Meremoth, of the priestly family of Hakkoz once excluded for want of a genealogy (Ezra 2:61-62), builds twice (vv. 4, 21).
3.theology:
No section of this wall is anyone's own work: thirty-one times the text says next to him or after him. The people of God are built together, and God keeps the names of those who work (Heb 6:10).

The Tower of Hananel (v. 1) and the Horse Gate (v. 28) are the two landmarks of Jeremiah's promise that the city would be rebuilt for the LORD, given in the same chapter as the new covenant (Jer 31:31-40). Nehemiah's wall was an instalment. The city that will not be plucked up or overthrown anymore forever is the one John saw, with names inscribed on its gates and foundations (Rev 21:12-14).
3.examples:
The high priest laid the first stones; his grandson married Sanballat's daughter.

A priest from a family once barred for want of a genealogy built two sections.

The nobles of Tekoa would not bend their necks; the men of Tekoa did two stretches.

Descendants of the Gibeonites who tricked Joshua built Jerusalem's wall.

Goldsmiths and perfumers lifted stone.

Shallum's daughters are the only women named on the wall.

A district ruler took the Dung Gate.

Men built opposite their own houses.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — They Built the Sheep Gate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliashib the high priest and the priests build and consecrate the Sheep Gate (v. 1); the men of Jericho, the sons of Hassenaah at the Fish Gate, Meremoth, Meshullam and Zadok work along the north wall, and the Tekoites repaired, but their nobles would not stoop to serve their Lord (vv. 2-5). Men of Gibeon and Mizpah, goldsmiths, perfumers and district rulers carry it west (vv. 6-11), and Shallum the son of Hallohesh, ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, repaired, he and his daughters (v. 12). The Valley Gate, the Dung Gate and the Fountain Gate are rebuilt round the southern end of the city (vv. 13-15).
verseByVerse.theology: Thirty-one times the chapter says next to him or after him. No section is anybody's own achievement; every stretch of wall joins someone else's.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Eliashib the high priest rose up with his brothers the priests, and they built the Sheep Gate. They consecrated it and set its doors. They consecrated it as far as the Tower of the Hundred, as far as the Tower of Hananel. And next to him the men of Jericho built. And next to them Zaccur the son of Imri built.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This chapter is a list, and it should be read as one: names, gates and stretches of wall, starting at the north-east corner by the temple and going round the city anticlockwise until it arrives back where it began. It is Nehemiah's work sheet. But nobody keeps a record like this unless every name on it mattered.

Then Eliashib the high priest rose up with his brothers the priests, and they built the Sheep Gate. They consecrated it and set its doors. The first man on the wall is the most senior man in Israel's religion, with his hands on the stones. And he begins at the Sheep Gate, through which the flocks came in for the sacrifices; it is the only gate in the list that is consecrated. Nearly five centuries later there was a pool by the Sheep Gate where Jesus found a man who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years and told him to get up and walk (John 5:2-8).

Hold one fact about Eliashib for later. In chapter 13 his grandson is married to the daughter of Sanballat (13:28), and an Eliashib, probably this one, has given Tobiah a room in the temple (13:4-7). The man who built the first gate let the enemy in through his own family. A good start is not the same as a faithful finish.

The Tower of the Hundred ... the Tower of Hananel. Remember that second name; it appears in a promise of Jeremiah's that this chapter begins to keep. And next to him the men of Jericho built — the city whose walls fell flat when Israel first entered the land sends men to put up Jerusalem's.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Hassenaah built the Fish Gate. They laid its beams and set its doors, its bolts, and its bars. And next to them Meremoth the son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz repaired. And next to them Meshullam the son of Berechiah, son of Meshezabel repaired. And next to them Zadok the son of Baana repaired. And next to them the Tekoites repaired, but their nobles would not stoop to serve their Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sons of Hassenaah build the Fish Gate, where fish came in from the coast, and hang its beams, doors, bolts and bars. And next to them Meremoth the son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz repaired.

Hakkoz. When the exiles first came home, the family of Hakkoz was one of three priestly families that could not find their names in the genealogies, and they were excluded from the priesthood as unclean (Ezra 2:61-62). Eighty years later Meremoth son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz, is the priest into whose hands Ezra weighed the temple's silver and gold (Ezra 8:33), and here he builds not one section of wall but two (v. 21). The family that nearly lost its place gave more than almost anyone.

And next to them the Tekoites repaired, but their nobles would not stoop to serve their Lord. Tekoa was a hill town some ten miles south, the town of the prophet Amos (Amos 1:1). Its ordinary men came in and worked. Its great men stood back. The phrase is literally that they would not bring their necks to the work, like an ox that will not take the yoke. The Tekoites answered by doing a second section (v. 27).

There is a yoke that is offered to every proud neck, and it is not heavy: Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matt 11:29). The one who says it stooped lower than any noble of Tekoa was ever asked to.

verseByVerse.quote: Joiada the son of Paseah and Meshullam the son of Besodeiah repaired the Gate of Yeshanah. They laid its beams and set its doors, its bolts, and its bars. And next to them repaired Melatiah the Gibeonite and Jadon the Meronothite, the men of Gibeon and of Mizpah, the seat of the governor of the province Beyond the River. Next to them Uzziel the son of Harhaiah, goldsmiths, repaired. Next to him Hananiah, one of the perfumers, repaired, and they restored Jerusalem as far as the Broad Wall. Next to them Rephaiah the son of Hur, ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, repaired. Next to them Jedaiah the son of Harumaph repaired opposite his house. And next to him Hattush the son of Hashabneiah repaired. Malchijah the son of Harim and Hasshub the son of Pahath-moab repaired another section and the Tower of the Ovens. Next to him Shallum the son of Hallohesh, ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, repaired, he and his daughters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Round the north-west corner and down the western side the names keep coming. Melatiah the Gibeonite and the men of Gibeon: descendants of the Canaanites who tricked Joshua and were made cutters of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD (Josh 9:27). The outsiders who were made servants of the altar are building its city's wall.

Uzziel the son of Harhaiah, goldsmiths ... Hananiah, one of the perfumers. Men who worked with fine gold and scented oils, with soft hands, lifting rough stone. Two rulers of half the district of Jerusalem take sections (vv. 9, 12). Jedaiah the son of Harumaph repaired opposite his house (v. 10), the first of several who built the stretch they would sleep behind.

Next to him Shallum the son of Hallohesh, ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, repaired, he and his daughters. They are the only women named on the wall, and they are named. Nothing else is known of them. They carried stone beside their father, and Scripture kept the fact.

That is what the list is for. God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name (Heb 6:10). Most of the work done for God in any generation is done by people whose names are forgotten within fifty years. Not one of them is forgotten by him.

verseByVerse.quote: Hanun and the inhabitants of Zanoah repaired the Valley Gate. They rebuilt it and set its doors, its bolts, and its bars, and repaired a thousand cubits of the wall, as far as the Dung Gate. Malchijah the son of Rechab, ruler of the district of Beth-haccherem, repaired the Dung Gate. He rebuilt it and set its doors, its bolts, and its bars. And Shallum the son of Col-hozeh, ruler of the district of Mizpah, repaired the Fountain Gate. He rebuilt it and covered it and set its doors, its bolts, and its bars. And he built the wall of the Pool of Shelah of the king's garden, as far as the stairs that go down from the city of David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hanun and the inhabitants of Zanoah repaired the Valley Gate ... and repaired a thousand cubits of the wall, as far as the Dung Gate. A thousand cubits is about five hundred yards, the only stretch in the chapter given a length, and a long one. Perhaps the wall there needed less, perhaps Zanoah simply sent many men.

Malchijah the son of Rechab, ruler of the district of Beth-haccherem, repaired the Dung Gate. The gate through which the city's refuse went out to the valley. A district ruler took it. Set him beside the nobles of Tekoa, who would not bend their necks at all.

Then the Fountain Gate, and the wall of the Pool of Shelah of the king's garden, as far as the stairs that go down from the city of David. Shelah is the pool Isaiah called Shiloah, the waters of Shiloah that flow gently (Isa 8:6), the pool the Gospels call Siloam. Jesus sent a blind man there: Go, wash in the pool of Siloam (which means Sent). So he went and washed and came back seeing (John 9:7).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–32 — Each Opposite His Own House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Up the eastern side: another Nehemiah, the Levites, the rulers of Keilah and Mizpah, Baruch, and Meremoth again, past the high priest's house (vv. 16-21). Priests, and householders opposite their house (vv. 22-24); the court of the guard, the temple servants on Ophel and the Water Gate, and the Tekoites again (vv. 25-27). Above the Horse Gate the priests repaired, each one opposite his own house (v. 28); the keeper of the East Gate, the goldsmiths and the merchants, until the circuit closes at the Sheep Gate where it began (vv. 29-32).
verseByVerse.theology: Seven times a man or a group repairs another section; several build the wall in front of their own door. Jeremiah had promised the city rebuilt from the Tower of Hananel to the corner of the Horse Gate (Jer 31:38-40), both of them named in this chapter, five verses after he promised the new covenant.

verseByVerse.quote: After him Nehemiah the son of Azbuk, ruler of half the district of Beth-zur, repaired to a point opposite the tombs of David, as far as the artificial pool, and as far as the house of the mighty men. After him the Levites repaired: Rehum the son of Bani. Next to him Hashabiah, ruler of half the district of Keilah, repaired for his district. After him their brothers repaired: Bavvai the son of Henadad, ruler of half the district of Keilah. Next to him Ezer the son of Jeshua, ruler of Mizpah, repaired another section opposite the ascent to the armory at the buttress. After him Baruch the son of Zabbai repaired another section from the buttress to the door of the house of Eliashib the high priest. After him Meremoth the son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz repaired another section from the door of the house of Eliashib to the end of the house of Eliashib. After him the priests, the men of the surrounding area, repaired. After them Benjamin and Hasshub repaired opposite their house. After them Azariah the son of Maaseiah, son of Ananiah repaired beside his own house. After him Binnui the son of Henadad repaired another section, from the house of Azariah to the buttress and to the corner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After him Nehemiah the son of Azbuk, ruler of half the district of Beth-zur, repaired — a different Nehemiah, not the governor telling the story. He worked near the tombs of David, the royal burial place inside the old city.

Levites, and rulers of Keilah and Mizpah (vv. 17-19). Then Baruch the son of Zabbai repaired another section from the buttress to the door of the house of Eliashib the high priest, and Meremoth of the family of Hakkoz does his second stretch, from the door of the house of Eliashib to the end of the house of Eliashib (vv. 20-21). The high priest's house was large enough to take a section of wall to itself, and the man from the family once shut out of the priesthood built in front of it.

After them Benjamin and Hasshub repaired opposite their house. After them Azariah ... repaired beside his own house. Nehemiah seems to have assigned men where they lived when he could. A man builds carefully when his own children sleep on the other side of the stones.

Seven times the chapter says someone repaired another section, a second stretch after finishing a first. Nobody was forced to do that. They saw a gap and filled it.

verseByVerse.quote: Palal the son of Uzai repaired opposite the buttress and the tower projecting from the upper house of the king at the court of the guard. After him Pedaiah the son of Parosh and the temple servants living on Ophel repaired to a point opposite the Water Gate on the east and the projecting tower. After him the Tekoites repaired another section opposite the great projecting tower as far as the wall of Ophel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Palal the son of Uzai repaired opposite the buttress and the tower projecting from the upper house of the king at the court of the guard. The court of the guard was where Jeremiah had been held prisoner while the Babylonians besieged the city (Jer 32:2), and where, with the enemy at the gates, he bought a field, because God had told him that houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land (Jer 32:15). Here, on the same spot, a century and a half later, men of that land are building.

The temple servants who lived on Ophel, the ridge south of the temple, work opposite the Water Gate on the east. It is in the square before that gate that the whole people will gather to hear Ezra read the law (8:1). And the Tekoites repaired another section. Their nobles had done nothing; the men of Tekoa did two sections.

verseByVerse.quote: Above the Horse Gate the priests repaired, each one opposite his own house. After them Zadok the son of Immer repaired opposite his own house. After him Shemaiah the son of Shecaniah, the keeper of the East Gate, repaired. After him Hananiah the son of Shelemiah and Hanun the sixth son of Zalaph repaired another section. After him Meshullam the son of Berechiah repaired opposite his chamber. After him Malchijah, one of the goldsmiths, repaired as far as the house of the temple servants and of the merchants, opposite the Muster Gate, and to the upper chamber of the corner. And between the upper chamber of the corner and the Sheep Gate the goldsmiths and the merchants repaired.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Above the Horse Gate the priests repaired, each one opposite his own house. Zadok son of Immer opposite his own house, the keeper of the East Gate, Meshullam opposite his chamber, Malchijah of the goldsmiths as far as the Muster Gate. And the last line: between the upper chamber of the corner and the Sheep Gate the goldsmiths and the merchants repaired. The circuit is closed. It ends at the Sheep Gate, where the high priest began.

Now set this chapter beside a promise. In the same chapter in which Jeremiah announced the new covenant, I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jer 31:33), he added this: the city shall be rebuilt for the LORD from the Tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate ... to the corner of the Horse Gate toward the east, shall be sacred to the LORD. It shall not be plucked up or overthrown anymore forever (Jer 31:38, 40). The Tower of Hananel is in verse 1 of this chapter; the Horse Gate is in verse 28. The people with their trowels were walking the line of Jeremiah's promise.

And yet not the whole of it. Jerusalem's walls came down again under Rome. The city that will never be plucked up is still to come, and when John saw it, its wall had names on it: on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel were inscribed, and on them were the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb (Rev 21:12, 14). The God who had the name of every builder on Nehemiah's wall written down builds his last city with names on its stones. And the Lamb whose apostles are written there is the one every sheep through that first gate had been pointing to.

4.title: Trowel and Sword
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when Sanballat heard that we were building the wall, he was angry and greatly enraged, and he jeered at the Jews.<sup>2</sup>And he said in the presence of his brothers and of the army of Samaria, "What are these feeble Jews doing? Will they restore it for themselves? Will they sacrifice? Will they finish up in a day? Will they revive the stones out of the heaps of rubbish, and burned ones at that?"<sup>3</sup>Tobiah the Ammonite was beside him, and he said, "Yes, what they are building— if a fox goes up on it he will break down their stone wall!"<sup>4</sup>Hear, O our God, for we are despised. Turn back their taunt on their own heads and give them up to be plundered in a land where they are captives.<sup>5</sup>Do not cover their guilt, and let not their sin be blotted out from your sight, for they have provoked you to anger in the presence of the builders.<sup>6</sup>So we built the wall. And all the wall was joined together to half its height, for the people had a mind to work.<sup>7</sup>But when Sanballat and Tobiah and the Arabs and the Ammonites and the Ashdodites heard that the repairing of the walls of Jerusalem was going forward and that the breaches were beginning to be closed, they were very angry.<sup>8</sup>And they all plotted together to come and fight against Jerusalem and to cause confusion in it.<sup>9</sup>And we prayed to our God and set a guard as a protection against them day and night.<sup>10</sup>In Judah it was said, "The strength of those who bear the burdens is failing. There is too much rubble. By ourselves we will not be able to rebuild the wall."<sup>11</sup>And our enemies said, "They will not know or see till we come among them and kill them and stop the work."<sup>12</sup>At that time the Jews who lived near them came from all directions and said to us ten times, "You must return to us."<sup>13</sup>So in the lowest parts of the space behind the wall, in open places, I stationed the people by their clans, with their swords, their spears, and their bows.<sup>14</sup>And I looked and arose and said to the nobles and to the officials and to the rest of the people, "Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your homes."<sup>15</sup>When our enemies heard that it was known to us and that God had frustrated their plan, we all returned to the wall, each to his work.<sup>16</sup>From that day on, half of my servants worked on construction, and half held the spears, shields, bows, and coats of mail. And the leaders stood behind the whole house of Judah,<sup>17</sup>who were building on the wall. Those who carried burdens were loaded in such a way that each labored on the work with one hand and held his weapon with the other.<sup>18</sup>And each of the builders had his sword strapped at his side while he built. The man who sounded the trumpet was beside me.<sup>19</sup>And I said to the nobles and to the officials and to the rest of the people, "The work is great and widely spread, and we are separated on the wall, far from one another.<sup>20</sup>In the place where you hear the sound of the trumpet, rally to us there. Our God will fight for us."<sup>21</sup>So we labored at the work, and half of them held the spears from the break of dawn until the stars came out.<sup>22</sup>I also said to the people at that time, "Let every man and his servant pass the night within Jerusalem, that they may be a guard for us by night and may labor by day."<sup>23</sup>So neither I nor my brothers nor my servants nor the men of the guard who followed me, none of us took off our clothes; each kept his weapon at his right hand.
4.overview: Sanballat mocks the feeble Jews in front of the army of Samaria — Will they revive the stones out of the heaps of rubbish, and burned ones at that? — and Tobiah says a fox could knock their wall down (vv. 1-3). Nehemiah prays God to turn the taunt back on them, in words borrowed from Jeremiah (vv. 4-5), and the wall rises to half its height, for the people had a mind to work (v. 6). The enemies, now on every side, plot an attack (vv. 7-8); the people pray and set a guard (v. 9); but inside Judah the burden-bearers are exhausted and relatives beg the men to come home (vv. 10-12). Nehemiah posts the families at the weak points and says Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight (vv. 13-14). God frustrates the plan (v. 15), and from then on they build with one hand and hold a weapon with the other, rally to the trumpet, and trust that Our God will fight for us (vv. 16-20), working dawn to dusk and sleeping in their clothes (vv. 21-23).
4.theology:
Prayer and prudence are never set against each other in this chapter: we prayed to our God and set a guard. Nor are God's fighting and theirs (vv. 14, 20). The sovereign God works through means, and his people's effort is the form his help takes.

Sanballat's scornful question — can burned stones be made alive? — is answered in Christ, the living stone rejected by men, who makes dead people into living stones built into God's house (1 Pet 2:4-5). And the imprecation of vv. 4-5 is handed to God, never carried out by hand; since the cross the believer's first prayer for an enemy is for his forgiveness (Acts 7:60), leaving justice to God (Rom 12:19).
4.examples:
Sanballat asked whether burned stones could be revived; God builds with nothing else.

Tobiah's fox is the animal Lamentations saw prowling over ruined Zion.

The wall was joined all the way round at half height.

The discouragement came from inside, at the halfway point, sung like a work song.

Their own families told them ten times to come home.

Nehemiah's cure for fear was the first line of his own prayer: great and awesome.

One hand on the work, one on the weapon.

The governor slept in his clothes like everyone else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Will They Revive the Stones?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sanballat hears that the wall is going up and jeers before the army of Samaria: What are these feeble Jews doing? ... Will they revive the stones out of the heaps of rubbish, and burned ones at that? (vv. 1-2). Tobiah adds that a fox would knock it down (v. 3). Nehemiah prays: Hear, O our God, for we are despised, and asks God not to cover their guilt (vv. 4-5). So we built the wall. And all the wall was joined together to half its height, for the people had a mind to work (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The first weapon is laughter. Nehemiah does not answer it; he takes it to God and goes back to the wall. The best reply to they cannot was a wall at half its height.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Sanballat heard that we were building the wall, he was angry and greatly enraged, and he jeered at the Jews. And he said in the presence of his brothers and of the army of Samaria, "What are these feeble Jews doing? Will they restore it for themselves? Will they sacrifice? Will they finish up in a day? Will they revive the stones out of the heaps of rubbish, and burned ones at that?" Tobiah the Ammonite was beside him, and he said, "Yes, what they are building— if a fox goes up on it he will break down their stone wall!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when Sanballat heard that we were building the wall, he was angry and greatly enraged, and he jeered at the Jews. He does it in public, in the presence of his brothers and of the army of Samaria, which means it is meant to be carried back to the builders. Laughter is cheaper than soldiers, and sometimes it works as well.

What are these feeble Jews doing? Will they restore it for themselves? Will they sacrifice? Will they finish up in a day? Will they revive the stones out of the heaps of rubbish, and burned ones at that? Five questions, each a small dose of doubt. Are you strong enough? Do you think you can pray it up? Do you know how long this will take? And the cleverest one last. Limestone that has been through a fire goes soft and crumbles; stones dug out of burned rubble were close to useless. He was not wrong about the stones.

But look at his verb. Revive means make alive, the word Ezra used when he thanked God for a little reviving (Ezra 9:8). Can dead stones come to life? Sanballat meant it as a joke. It is, in fact, exactly what God does. As you come to him, a living stone rejected by men ... you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house (1 Pet 2:4-5). God builds with burned and broken material; it is the only material he has ever had.

Tobiah the Ammonite was beside him, and he said, Yes, what they are building — if a fox goes up on it he will break down their stone wall! A fox weighs next to nothing. And the fox was the animal of Jerusalem's ruin: Mount Zion which lies desolate; jackals prowl over it (Lam 5:18), the same creature in Hebrew. Tobiah is saying that Zion is still what Lamentations said it was, a place for foxes.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, O our God, for we are despised. Turn back their taunt on their own heads and give them up to be plundered in a land where they are captives. Do not cover their guilt, and let not their sin be blotted out from your sight, for they have provoked you to anger in the presence of the builders.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear, O our God, for we are despised. Turn back their taunt on their own heads and give them up to be plundered in a land where they are captives. Do not cover their guilt, and let not their sin be blotted out from your sight, for they have provoked you to anger in the presence of the builders.

Nehemiah does not answer Sanballat. He answers God. Taunt is the word for the shame of 1:3, and he asks God to send it back where it came from. And the second sentence is borrowed from Jeremiah, whose enemies were plotting to kill him: Forgive not their iniquity, nor blot out their sin from your sight (Jer 18:23).

A Christian reading this may be troubled, and should be allowed to ask. How does it sit with Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34)? Three things, plainly. First, Nehemiah takes no revenge; he hands the matter to God, which is exactly what the New Testament commands: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Rom 12:19). Second, his reason is not a private insult but that they provoked you to anger — they were setting themselves against God's own work. Third, the cry for justice is not abolished in the New Testament; the martyrs under the altar still pray how long before you will judge and avenge our blood? (Rev 6:10).

But the Christian's first prayer for an enemy is now Stephen's: Lord, do not hold this sin against them (Acts 7:60). If someone has wronged you badly, you may tell God the whole of it and ask him to see it and deal justly. You may not take it into your own hands, and you must pray for their repentance before you pray for anything else. Justice for the one who never repents is safe with God.

verseByVerse.quote: So we built the wall. And all the wall was joined together to half its height, for the people had a mind to work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So we built the wall. And all the wall was joined together to half its height, for the people had a mind to work.

So we built. That is the whole of Nehemiah's reply to the five questions and the fox. He prayed, and then he laid the next stone. All the wall was joined together: the separate gangs of chapter 3 had met, and there was now one continuous wall right round the city, at half height.

A mind to work is, literally, a heart to work. The people's hearts were in it. Mockery can take the heart out of a people faster than any army; here it did not.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The enemies now come from every side, and plot to attack and cause confusion (vv. 7-8). We prayed to our God and set a guard (v. 9). But inside Judah the burden-bearers are exhausted and the rubble seems endless (v. 10); the enemy boasts of a surprise attack (v. 11), and Jews from the villages urge their families home ten times over (v. 12). Nehemiah posts the people by clans with swords, spears and bows (v. 13) and says, Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your homes (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The cure Nehemiah gives for fear is a memory. The words great and awesome are the first words of his own prayer in 1:5. What he had said to God, he now says to the people.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Sanballat and Tobiah and the Arabs and the Ammonites and the Ashdodites heard that the repairing of the walls of Jerusalem was going forward and that the breaches were beginning to be closed, they were very angry. And they all plotted together to come and fight against Jerusalem and to cause confusion in it. And we prayed to our God and set a guard as a protection against them day and night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when Sanballat and Tobiah and the Arabs and the Ammonites and the Ashdodites heard that the repairing of the walls of Jerusalem was going forward and that the breaches were beginning to be closed, they were very angry.

Look at the map. Sanballat's Samaria to the north; Tobiah's Ammonites to the east across the Jordan; the Arabs to the south; and now the Ashdodites, from the old Philistine coast, to the west. In chapter 2 there were three enemies. Now Jerusalem is surrounded on every side. The laughter stopped when the gaps began to close, and the plotting began: to come and fight against Jerusalem and to cause confusion in it.

And we prayed to our God and set a guard as a protection against them day and night. Both. They did not pray instead of posting sentries, and they did not post sentries instead of praying. Faith that refuses to lock the door is not faith, and a locked door without prayer is not safety.

verseByVerse.quote: In Judah it was said, "The strength of those who bear the burdens is failing. There is too much rubble. By ourselves we will not be able to rebuild the wall." And our enemies said, "They will not know or see till we come among them and kill them and stop the work." At that time the Jews who lived near them came from all directions and said to us ten times, "You must return to us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Judah it was said, The strength of those who bear the burdens is failing. There is too much rubble. By ourselves we will not be able to rebuild the wall.

This time the voice is not Sanballat's. It is Judah's own. In Hebrew the line runs with the rhythm of a work song, the kind of chant men carry baskets to, and it has turned into a lament. The men carrying earth and stone up the slope were spent, and the heaps of rubble never seemed to get smaller.

Notice when it came: straight after half its height. The start of a great work has its own energy, and the end has the finish line in sight. The middle is where the strength goes. Many readers are at a halfway point of something just now — a marriage in its hard years, a long illness, children not yet grown, a work for God with no end in sight — and know this sentence from the inside. By ourselves we will not be able. That is true. It was never meant to be done by themselves.

Then the enemy boasts that they will come among the builders unseen and kill them (v. 11), and the Jews who lived out near the enemy villages come in from all directions and said to us ten times, You must return to us. Families calling their men home before the attack. The hardest pressure to go back often comes from people who love you.

verseByVerse.quote: So in the lowest parts of the space behind the wall, in open places, I stationed the people by their clans, with their swords, their spears, and their bows. And I looked and arose and said to the nobles and to the officials and to the rest of the people, "Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your homes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So in the lowest parts of the space behind the wall, in open places, I stationed the people by their clans, with their swords, their spears, and their bows. He put them where the wall was lowest and where the enemy could see them, and he put them there by families. A man stands his ground when his own brothers are beside him.

And I looked and arose and said to the nobles and to the officials and to the rest of the people, Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your homes.

Great and awesome. Those are the first words of Nehemiah's prayer in Susa: the great and awesome God who keeps covenant (1:5). Months of praying had put them into his mouth, and now he gives them to the people. The cure he offers for fear is not a better estimate of the enemy. It is a memory of God. Fear grows when the enemy fills the whole view; it shrinks when the Lord is remembered for what he is.

And then, fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your homes. Remembering God did not make the fighting unnecessary. It made it possible.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — Our God Will Fight for Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God frustrates the plan and the people go back each to his work (v. 15). From then on half the men work and half stand armed; each labored on the work with one hand and held his weapon with the other, and every builder wears a sword (vv. 16-18). The trumpeter stands beside Nehemiah: In the place where you hear the sound of the trumpet, rally to us there. Our God will fight for us (vv. 19-20). They work from dawn until the stars come out, sleep inside the city, and never take off their clothes (vv. 21-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Fight for your brothers (v. 14) and our God will fight for us (v. 20) in the same speech. Moses had said the second at the Red Sea (Exod 14:14). God's fighting did not make theirs unnecessary; theirs did not make his unnecessary.

verseByVerse.quote: When our enemies heard that it was known to us and that God had frustrated their plan, we all returned to the wall, each to his work. From that day on, half of my servants worked on construction, and half held the spears, shields, bows, and coats of mail. And the leaders stood behind the whole house of Judah, who were building on the wall. Those who carried burdens were loaded in such a way that each labored on the work with one hand and held his weapon with the other. And each of the builders had his sword strapped at his side while he built. The man who sounded the trumpet was beside me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When our enemies heard that it was known to us and that God had frustrated their plan, we all returned to the wall, each to his work. The surprise attack depended on surprise, and it was lost. Nehemiah credits the whole thing to God: God had frustrated their plan. And the result is not a celebration but a return to work, each to his work, back to the particular stretch of wall that was his.

From that day the work changed shape. Half of Nehemiah's own men worked and half stood armed with spears, shields, bows and mail. Those who carried burdens were loaded in such a way that each labored on the work with one hand and held his weapon with the other. And each of the builders had his sword strapped at his side while he built. A man with a basket of stone on one shoulder and a spear in the other hand. A mason laying blocks with a sword knocking against his leg.

It is a true picture of God's people in this world, and it needs one correction before it is used. The church is not given a literal sword: the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh (2 Cor 10:4). Its sword is the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph 6:17). But the posture is the same. We build, and we guard what we build, and we never get a season in which only one of those is needed.

verseByVerse.quote: And I said to the nobles and to the officials and to the rest of the people, "The work is great and widely spread, and we are separated on the wall, far from one another. In the place where you hear the sound of the trumpet, rally to us there. Our God will fight for us." So we labored at the work, and half of them held the spears from the break of dawn until the stars came out. I also said to the people at that time, "Let every man and his servant pass the night within Jerusalem, that they may be a guard for us by night and may labor by day." So neither I nor my brothers nor my servants nor the men of the guard who followed me, none of us took off our clothes; each kept his weapon at his right hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The work is great and widely spread, and we are separated on the wall, far from one another. In the place where you hear the sound of the trumpet, rally to us there. Our God will fight for us. The trumpeter stood beside Nehemiah. Wherever the attack came, one blast would bring the whole wall running.

Our God will fight for us. Moses said it at the Red Sea: The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent (Exod 14:14). But six verses earlier Nehemiah told these same men to fight for your brothers (v. 14). Both are true, and neither cancels the other. God fights, and his people fight, and when they win it is still God's victory.

So we labored at the work, and half of them held the spears from the break of dawn until the stars came out. Everyone slept inside the city so there would be guards by night and workers by day (v. 22). So neither I nor my brothers nor my servants nor the men of the guard who followed me, none of us took off our clothes. The governor slept in his clothes with his weapon beside him, like every other man on the wall.

That is a leader who asks nothing he does not do. Ours went further. He did not only share his people's watch; he took on himself the attack they could not survive, and won it alone. If God is for us, who can be against us? (Rom 8:31).

5.title: The Enemy Within
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there arose a great outcry of the people and of their wives against their Jewish brothers.<sup>2</sup>For there were those who said, "With our sons and our daughters, we are many. So let us get grain, that we may eat and keep alive."<sup>3</sup>There were also those who said, "We are mortgaging our fields, our vineyards, and our houses to get grain because of the famine."<sup>4</sup>And there were those who said, "We have borrowed money for the king's tax on our fields and our vineyards.<sup>5</sup>Now our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers, our children are as their children. Yet we are forcing our sons and our daughters to be slaves, and some of our daughters have already been enslaved, but it is not in our power to help it, for other men have our fields and our vineyards."<sup>6</sup>I was very angry when I heard their outcry and these words.<sup>7</sup>I took counsel with myself, and I brought charges against the nobles and the officials. I said to them, "You are exacting interest, each from his brother." And I held a great assembly against them<sup>8</sup>and said to them, "We, as far as we are able, have bought back our Jewish brothers who have been sold to the nations, but you even sell your brothers that they may be sold to us!" They were silent and could not find a word to say.<sup>9</sup>So I said, "The thing that you are doing is not good. Ought you not to walk in the fear of our God to prevent the taunts of the nations our enemies?<sup>10</sup>Moreover, I and my brothers and my servants are lending them money and grain. Let us abandon this exacting of interest.<sup>11</sup>Return to them this very day their fields, their vineyards, their olive orchards, and their houses, and the percentage of money, grain, wine, and oil that you have been exacting from them."<sup>12</sup>Then they said, "We will restore these and require nothing from them. We will do as you say." And I called the priests and made them swear to do as they had promised.<sup>13</sup>I also shook out the fold of my garment and said, "So may God shake out every man from his house and from his labor who does not keep this promise. So may he be shaken out and emptied." And all the assembly said "Amen" and praised the LORD. And the people did as they had promised.<sup>14</sup>Moreover, from the time that I was appointed to be their governor in the land of Judah, from the twentieth year to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes the king, twelve years, neither I nor my brothers ate the food allowance of the governor.<sup>15</sup>The former governors who were before me laid heavy burdens on the people and took from them for their daily ration forty shekels of silver. Even their servants lorded it over the people. But I did not do so, because of the fear of God.<sup>16</sup>I also persevered in the work on this wall, and we acquired no land, and all my servants were gathered there for the work.<sup>17</sup>Moreover, there were at my table 150 men, Jews and officials, besides those who came to us from the nations that were around us.<sup>18</sup>Now what was prepared at my expense for each day was one ox and six choice sheep and birds, and every ten days all kinds of wine in abundance. Yet for all this I did not demand the food allowance of the governor, because the service was too heavy on this people.<sup>19</sup>Remember for my good, O my God, all that I have done for this people.
5.overview: With the wall half-built, a great outcry rises against the Jews' own nobles. Families are hungry, fields are mortgaged in a famine, money has been borrowed for the king's tax, and children are being sold into slavery to pay the lenders (vv. 1-5). Nehemiah is very angry, thinks it through, and publicly charges the nobles with exacting interest from their brothers and selling Jews whom he had been buying back (vv. 6-8). He calls them to the fear of our God — the phrase of the interest law itself (Lev 25:36) — lest they hand the enemies their taunt, and, including his own household, demands everything returned that day (vv. 9-11). They swear before the priests; he shakes out his garment as a curse on oath-breakers; the assembly says Amen and praises the LORD (vv. 12-13). Then Nehemiah records that for twelve years as governor he took no allowance, bought no land, and fed 150 men a day from his own purse, because of the fear of God, and asks God to remember it (vv. 14-19).
5.theology:
How God's people handle money among themselves is covenant faithfulness, not a side issue. The law forbade interest from a poor brother because God had brought them all out of slavery (Lev 25:36-42); to re-enslave a brother was to undo the Exodus. And a leader's authority to call others to that standard rests on his own practice: Nehemiah demanded the fear of God and had lived by it for twelve years.

The rulers of the nations lord it over their people; Nehemiah would not, and Christ, though rich, became poor and gave his life as a ransom for many (Matt 20:25-28; 2 Cor 8:9). Remember me, O my God, for good is the prayer of a servant who knows his record is safe with God and his standing rests on God's steadfast love (13:22).
5.examples:
The loudest cry in the besieged city was against fellow Jews.

First the crop, then the field, then the daughter.

Nehemiah was very angry, and took counsel with himself before he spoke.

We buy our brothers back; you sell them.

He said let us stop — his own household had been lending too.

He shook his pocket out as a curse on anyone who broke the oath.

In twelve years of famine and taxes, the governor bought no land.

He fed 150 men a day and never drew his allowance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Let Us Abandon This Exacting of Interest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A great outcry goes up against their Jewish brothers: families hungry, fields mortgaged for grain in a famine, money borrowed for the king's tax, and some of our daughters have already been enslaved (vv. 1-5). Nehemiah is very angry, thinks before he speaks, and charges the nobles: You are exacting interest, each from his brother (vv. 6-7). We bought our brothers back from the nations; you sell them (v. 8). Ought you not to walk in the fear of our God to prevent the taunts of the nations our enemies? (v. 9). He demands everything returned this very day (vv. 10-11); they swear before the priests, he shakes out his garment as a curse on any who break the oath, and all the assembly said Amen and praised the LORD (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: The most dangerous enemy of this chapter is not Sanballat. It is a brother with a ledger. The law had forbidden interest from a poor brother with the words fear your God (Lev 25:36), and that is exactly the phrase Nehemiah reaches for.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there arose a great outcry of the people and of their wives against their Jewish brothers. For there were those who said, "With our sons and our daughters, we are many. So let us get grain, that we may eat and keep alive." There were also those who said, "We are mortgaging our fields, our vineyards, and our houses to get grain because of the famine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there arose a great outcry of the people and of their wives against their Jewish brothers.

The wall is at half height, the enemy is circling, and the loudest cry in Jerusalem is not against Sanballat. It is against fellow Jews. Outcry is the word of Exodus, where God said, I have surely seen the affliction of my people ... and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters (Exod 3:7). And the law had joined that cry to money-lending in so many words: If you lend money to any of my people with you who is poor, you shall not ... exact interest from him ... And if he cries to me, I will hear, for I am compassionate (Exod 22:25, 27). The people redeemed from taskmasters had taskmasters again, and they were their own brothers.

Notice and of their wives. The women who had to feed the children were crying loudest. A famine had come (v. 3), the king's tax had not stopped for it (v. 4), and the families at the bottom were going under.

The complaints come in a rising order. With our sons and our daughters, we are many. So let us get grain, that we may eat and keep alive: we simply need food. Then, We are mortgaging our fields, our vineyards, and our houses to get grain because of the famine: we are pledging everything we own to eat this year.

verseByVerse.quote: And there were those who said, "We have borrowed money for the king's tax on our fields and our vineyards. Now our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers, our children are as their children. Yet we are forcing our sons and our daughters to be slaves, and some of our daughters have already been enslaved, but it is not in our power to help it, for other men have our fields and our vineyards."
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have borrowed money for the king's tax on our fields and our vineyards. Persia taxed the land in silver whether the harvest came or not. A farmer with no crop and a tax demand borrowed from whoever had silver, and the ones who had silver were the nobles.

Now our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers, our children are as their children. Yet we are forcing our sons and our daughters to be slaves, and some of our daughters have already been enslaved, but it is not in our power to help it, for other men have our fields and our vineyards.

That is the bottom of the spiral. First the crop, then the field, then the child. A father handing his daughter over as a servant to pay a debt to a man who worships at the same altar. Our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers: we are the same blood; my child is worth what his child is worth. And there is no way back, because the fields that could have redeemed her belong to someone else now.

Measure that against the wall going up outside. You can build a magnificent defence round a people and still let them be devoured from inside it.

verseByVerse.quote: I was very angry when I heard their outcry and these words. I took counsel with myself, and I brought charges against the nobles and the officials. I said to them, "You are exacting interest, each from his brother." And I held a great assembly against them and said to them, "We, as far as we are able, have bought back our Jewish brothers who have been sold to the nations, but you even sell your brothers that they may be sold to us!" They were silent and could not find a word to say.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I was very angry when I heard their outcry and these words. I took counsel with myself. Both halves matter. He was very angry, and the text does not apologise for it; some things ought to make a godly man angry, and a father selling his daughter to pay interest to a rich Jew is one of them. But then he took counsel with himself — literally, his heart deliberated within him. The anger went through his heart before it went through his mouth.

Here is a test to run before your next angry word. Nehemiah's anger had three marks: it was on someone else's behalf, not his own; it waited until it had thought; and it went straight to the people responsible, openly. Anger on my own account, unthought, and expressed to everyone except the person concerned, has none of the three.

I brought charges against the nobles and the officials. I said to them, You are exacting interest, each from his brother. Each from his brother. The law had said it: you shall not charge interest on loans to your brother (Deut 23:19).

Then, before a great assembly: We, as far as we are able, have bought back our Jewish brothers who have been sold to the nations, but you even sell your brothers that they may be sold to us! Nehemiah and others had been spending their own silver redeeming Jews sold abroad as slaves, and the nobles were selling Jews into slavery at home, so that they would have to be bought back again. The law had forbidden it for a reason that goes back to the Exodus: they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt; they shall not be sold as slaves (Lev 25:42). They were silent and could not find a word to say.

verseByVerse.quote: So I said, "The thing that you are doing is not good. Ought you not to walk in the fear of our God to prevent the taunts of the nations our enemies? Moreover, I and my brothers and my servants are lending them money and grain. Let us abandon this exacting of interest. Return to them this very day their fields, their vineyards, their olive orchards, and their houses, and the percentage of money, grain, wine, and oil that you have been exacting from them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I said, The thing that you are doing is not good. Ought you not to walk in the fear of our God to prevent the taunts of the nations our enemies?

The fear of our God. That phrase is in the very law they were breaking: Take no interest from him or profit, but fear your God, that your brother may live beside you (Lev 25:36). Moses had set the fear of God against the moneylender's profit, and Nehemiah simply quotes the reason back.

And the taunts of the nations is the word the book began with, the shame of 1:3 and the derision of 2:17. The whole wall was being built to silence the sneer of the neighbours. The nobles were handing it back to them from the inside. What would Sanballat say of a God whose people sold each other's children?

Moreover, I and my brothers and my servants are lending them money and grain. Let us abandon this exacting of interest. Let us. Nehemiah's own household had been lending too, and he does not exempt it. As in his first prayer — even I and my father's house have sinned (1:6) — he puts his own name inside the rebuke.

Return to them this very day their fields, their vineyards, their olive orchards, and their houses, and the percentage of money, grain, wine, and oil that you have been exacting from them. The percentage is literally the hundredth, probably one per cent a month. Not a gradual easing. The land back and the interest back, today.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they said, "We will restore these and require nothing from them. We will do as you say." And I called the priests and made them swear to do as they had promised. I also shook out the fold of my garment and said, "So may God shake out every man from his house and from his labor who does not keep this promise. So may he be shaken out and emptied." And all the assembly said "Amen" and praised the LORD. And the people did as they had promised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they said, We will restore these and require nothing from them. We will do as you say. To their great credit, they did not argue. But Nehemiah had seen promises made in a crowded room evaporate on the way home. I called the priests and made them swear to do as they had promised.

I also shook out the fold of my garment and said, So may God shake out every man from his house and from his labor who does not keep this promise. So may he be shaken out and emptied. The fold of a robe was a man's pocket. Nehemiah turned his inside out and shook it empty in front of them: that is what God will do to the house of the man who breaks this oath. Paul made the same gesture at Corinth, when the synagogue turned on him: he shook out his garments and said to them, Your blood be on your own heads! (Acts 18:6).

And all the assembly said Amen and praised the LORD. And the people did as they had promised. A debt cancellation ended in worship. When wrong money is given back, God is praised; it is one of the plainest tests of whether a revival is real.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–19 — Because of the Fear of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For twelve years as governor, Nehemiah and his brothers never took the governor's food allowance (v. 14). Earlier governors had laid heavy burdens on the people, and even their servants lorded it over the people. But I did not do so, because of the fear of God (v. 15). He worked on the wall, bought no land (v. 16), and fed 150 men daily at his own expense, besides visitors from the nations (vv. 17-18). Remember for my good, O my God, all that I have done for this people (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The first of Nehemiah's four prayers to be remembered (5:19; 13:14, 22, 31). It is not a claim to have earned God's favour; the man who prays it will also ask to be spared according to the greatness of your steadfast love (13:22).

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, from the time that I was appointed to be their governor in the land of Judah, from the twentieth year to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes the king, twelve years, neither I nor my brothers ate the food allowance of the governor. The former governors who were before me laid heavy burdens on the people and took from them for their daily ration forty shekels of silver. Even their servants lorded it over the people. But I did not do so, because of the fear of God. I also persevered in the work on this wall, and we acquired no land, and all my servants were gathered there for the work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moreover, from the time that I was appointed to be their governor in the land of Judah, from the twentieth year to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes the king, twelve years, neither I nor my brothers ate the food allowance of the governor. The governor was entitled to be fed by the province. For twelve years Nehemiah drew nothing.

The former governors who were before me laid heavy burdens on the people and took from them for their daily ration forty shekels of silver. Even their servants lorded it over the people. But I did not do so, because of the fear of God.

It is the same fear he had just demanded of the nobles (v. 9). He was not asking of them anything he had not already done for twelve years. And lorded it over is exactly what Jesus said rulers do: You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them ... It shall not be so among you ... even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Matt 20:25-28).

I also persevered in the work on this wall, and we acquired no land. In a famine, with families mortgaging their fields, land could be had for almost nothing. The governor bought none. He kept his own servants on the wall, not on estates.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, there were at my table 150 men, Jews and officials, besides those who came to us from the nations that were around us. Now what was prepared at my expense for each day was one ox and six choice sheep and birds, and every ten days all kinds of wine in abundance. Yet for all this I did not demand the food allowance of the governor, because the service was too heavy on this people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moreover, there were at my table 150 men, Jews and officials, besides those who came to us from the nations that were around us. A governor's table was an office of state: officials to feed, envoys from the neighbouring peoples to entertain. Every day one ox and six choice sheep and birds, and every ten days all kinds of wine in abundance. That is a great deal of meat, and Nehemiah paid for it.

Yet for all this I did not demand the food allowance of the governor, because the service was too heavy on this people. The service is the labour on the wall. Men who were carrying stone all day, with a sword at their side and a famine at home, were not going to be taxed to feed the governor as well.

There is a greater Governor who did far more than decline an allowance. For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Cor 8:9). Nehemiah bought back brothers sold to the nations with his silver (v. 8). Christ bought back his people with himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember for my good, O my God, all that I have done for this people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember for my good, O my God, all that I have done for this people.

This is the first of four such prayers in the book (5:19; 13:14, 22, 31), and a reader may wonder whether it is a little self-regarding. It is not a bid for salvation. When Nehemiah prays it again in chapter 13 he adds, and spare me according to the greatness of your steadfast love (13:22). He knows he will be kept by mercy. What he asks is that the service he gave, unseen and unpaid, not be lost.

He did not publish his twelve years of self-denial to the people or ask them for thanks. He told God. The governor who went without had a Master who would not forget. God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name (Heb 6:10). Nothing given up for his people's sake, in an office or a kitchen or a hospital corridor, goes unrecorded.

6.title: Finished
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when Sanballat and Tobiah and Geshem the Arab and the rest of our enemies heard that I had built the wall and that there was no breach left in it (although up to that time I had not set up the doors in the gates),<sup>2</sup>Sanballat and Geshem sent to me, saying, "Come and let us meet together at Hakkephirim in the plain of Ono." But they intended to do me harm.<sup>3</sup>And I sent messengers to them, saying, "I am doing a great work and I cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it and come down to you?"<sup>4</sup>And they sent to me four times in this way, and I answered them in the same manner.<sup>5</sup>In the same way Sanballat for the fifth time sent his servant to me with an open letter in his hand.<sup>6</sup>In it was written, "It is reported among the nations, and Geshem also says it, that you and the Jews intend to rebel; that is why you are building the wall. And according to these reports you wish to become their king.<sup>7</sup>And you have also set up prophets to proclaim concerning you in Jerusalem, 'There is a king in Judah.' And now the king will hear of these reports. So now come and let us take counsel together."<sup>8</sup>Then I sent to him, saying, "No such things as you say have been done, for you are inventing them out of your own mind."<sup>9</sup>For they all wanted to frighten us, thinking, "Their hands will drop from the work, and it will not be done." But now, O God, strengthen my hands.<sup>10</sup>Now when I went into the house of Shemaiah the son of Delaiah, son of Mehetabel, who was confined to his home, he said, "Let us meet together in the house of God, within the temple. Let us close the doors of the temple, for they are coming to kill you. They are coming to kill you by night."<sup>11</sup>But I said, "Should such a man as I run away? And what man such as I could go into the temple and live? I will not go in."<sup>12</sup>And I understood and saw that God had not sent him, but he had pronounced the prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him.<sup>13</sup>For this purpose he was hired, that I should be afraid and act in this way and sin, and so they could give me a bad name in order to taunt me.<sup>14</sup>Remember Tobiah and Sanballat, O my God, according to these things that they did, and also the prophetess Noadiah and the rest of the prophets who wanted to make me afraid.<sup>15</sup>So the wall was finished on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty-two days.<sup>16</sup>And when all our enemies heard of it, all the nations around us were afraid and fell greatly in their own esteem, for they perceived that this work had been accomplished with the help of our God.<sup>17</sup>Moreover, in those days the nobles of Judah sent many letters to Tobiah, and Tobiah's letters came to them.<sup>18</sup>For many in Judah were bound by oath to him, because he was the son-in-law of Shecaniah the son of Arah: and his son Jehohanan had taken the daughter of Meshullam the son of Berechiah as his wife.<sup>19</sup>Also they spoke of his good deeds in my presence and reported my words to him. And Tobiah sent letters to make me afraid.
6.overview: With the wall complete but the doors not yet hung, the enemies turn on Nehemiah himself. Sanballat and Geshem invite him four times to a meeting at Ono, meaning him harm; four times he answers, I am doing a great work and I cannot come down (vv. 1-4). A fifth message, an open letter, accuses him of plotting rebellion and kingship, with prophets proclaiming There is a king in Judah; he denies it in one sentence and prays, O God, strengthen my hands (vv. 5-9). Shemaiah, a hired prophet, urges him to hide in the temple from assassins; he refuses to run or to enter where a layman may not go, and sees that God had not sent the man (vv. 10-14). The wall is finished on 25 Elul in fifty-two days, and the nations are afraid, for they perceived that this work had been accomplished with the help of our God (vv. 15-16). But Tobiah has marriage ties with leading Jewish families, including the family of a man who built two sections of the wall, and his letters keep coming (vv. 17-19).
6.theology:
God's work is finished by God's help, and even his enemies are made to see it (v. 16; Ps 126:2). A word that urges sin for safety's sake is not from God, however it is dressed (v. 12; 1 John 4:1).

The slander that Nehemiah meant to be king was false; the promise behind it was not. Zechariah had announced to Jerusalem that her King was coming (Zech 9:9), and he came, and died under the charge Sanballat invented: the King of the Jews (John 19:19). He is the builder whose city has no enemy inside its walls (Rev 21:27).
6.examples:
I am doing a great work and I cannot come down — four times.

The fifth letter was open, so the slander was published before it was answered.

He answered a long lie with a single sentence.

The prophet told him to hide in the holy place; he would not buy safety with a sin.

The enemies set out to make him afraid, and ended up afraid themselves.

Fifty-two days.

A man who built two sections of the wall had married his daughter into Tobiah's family.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — I Am Doing a Great Work
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wall is up with no breach left, though the doors are not yet hung (v. 1). Sanballat and Geshem invite Nehemiah to a meeting in the plain of Ono, meaning him harm; he replies, I am doing a great work and I cannot come down, four times (vv. 2-4). The fifth message is an open letter: the Jews mean to rebel, Nehemiah means to be king, and prophets are proclaiming There is a king in Judah (vv. 5-7). No such things as you say have been done, for you are inventing them out of your own mind (v. 8). They meant to frighten the builders until their hands dropped. But now, O God, strengthen my hands (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: When the wall could not be stopped, the enemy aimed at the man: first his time, then his reputation. Nehemiah gave neither up. He declined the meeting, denied the lie in one sentence, and prayed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Sanballat and Tobiah and Geshem the Arab and the rest of our enemies heard that I had built the wall and that there was no breach left in it (although up to that time I had not set up the doors in the gates), Sanballat and Geshem sent to me, saying, "Come and let us meet together at Hakkephirim in the plain of Ono." But they intended to do me harm. And I sent messengers to them, saying, "I am doing a great work and I cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it and come down to you?" And they sent to me four times in this way, and I answered them in the same manner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when Sanballat and Tobiah and Geshem the Arab and the rest of our enemies heard that I had built the wall and that there was no breach left in it (although up to that time I had not set up the doors in the gates). The circle is closed. Only the gates stand open, waiting for their doors. Everything the enemy has tried has failed, so the enemy changes target. If the wall cannot be stopped, perhaps the builder can.

Come and let us meet together at Hakkephirim in the plain of Ono. But they intended to do me harm. Ono lay out in the lowlands toward the coast, a long day's ride from Jerusalem, on neutral ground. It sounded like diplomacy. It was a trap, and Nehemiah knew it.

I am doing a great work and I cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it and come down to you? Ono was literally down, off the hills. But the words carry more than geography. The work was great because it was God's, and a man given a great work cannot spend his days in meetings with people who want it to fail.

And they sent to me four times in this way, and I answered them in the same manner. Four times the same invitation; four times the same answer. Persistence is the enemy's method, and it works on most of us: the fourth request feels unreasonable to refuse. Here is a question to ask of the invitations crowding your own calendar. Which of them would take you off the wall God has given you? Not everything that asks for your time is wicked. Some of it is only designed, by someone, to make sure the great work does not get done.

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way Sanballat for the fifth time sent his servant to me with an open letter in his hand. In it was written, "It is reported among the nations, and Geshem also says it, that you and the Jews intend to rebel; that is why you are building the wall. And according to these reports you wish to become their king. And you have also set up prophets to proclaim concerning you in Jerusalem, 'There is a king in Judah.' And now the king will hear of these reports. So now come and let us take counsel together." Then I sent to him, saying, "No such things as you say have been done, for you are inventing them out of your own mind." For they all wanted to frighten us, thinking, "Their hands will drop from the work, and it will not be done." But now, O God, strengthen my hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the same way Sanballat for the fifth time sent his servant to me with an open letter in his hand. An open letter: unsealed, read by the servant who carried it and by anyone else along the road. The slander had been published before Nehemiah read it.

It is reported among the nations, and Geshem also says it, that you and the Jews intend to rebel; that is why you are building the wall. And according to these reports you wish to become their king. And you have also set up prophets to proclaim concerning you in Jerusalem, There is a king in Judah. It is reported, and Geshem also says it: gossip citing gossip as its source. And a threat: now the king will hear of these reports.

The lie was false about Nehemiah, and he never claimed a crown. But it was true about God's promise. A prophet had proclaimed in Jerusalem two generations earlier, Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! ... Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey (Zech 9:9). There was a King coming to Judah. And when he came, the charge Sanballat invented against Nehemiah was the charge nailed over his head: Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews (John 19:19).

No such things as you say have been done, for you are inventing them out of your own mind. One sentence. He did not write a defence or gather testimonials; a man who answers every slander at length has already stopped building. For they all wanted to frighten us, thinking, Their hands will drop from the work, and it will not be done. But now, O God, strengthen my hands. When he first called them to build, they strengthened their hands for the good work (2:18). Now the enemy wants those hands to fall, and he asks God to strengthen them. The New Testament prays the same for tired believers: lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees (Heb 12:12).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–19 — With the Help of Our God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Shemaiah, a prophet paid by Tobiah and Sanballat, urges Nehemiah to hide from assassins inside the temple (v. 10). Should such a man as I run away? And what man such as I could go into the temple and live? I will not go in (vv. 11-13). Nehemiah asks God to remember his enemies and the false prophets (v. 14). So the wall was finished on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty-two days, and the nations perceived that this work had been accomplished with the help of our God (vv. 15-16). But Tobiah is related by marriage to leading families in Judah, the nobles correspond with him, and his letters keep coming (vv. 17-19).
verseByVerse.theology: The enemies set out to make Nehemiah afraid (vv. 9, 13, 14, 19), and in the end it was the nations who were afraid (v. 16). Those who had laughed at the feeble Jews (4:2) now saw God in the finished wall.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when I went into the house of Shemaiah the son of Delaiah, son of Mehetabel, who was confined to his home, he said, "Let us meet together in the house of God, within the temple. Let us close the doors of the temple, for they are coming to kill you. They are coming to kill you by night." But I said, "Should such a man as I run away? And what man such as I could go into the temple and live? I will not go in."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when I went into the house of Shemaiah the son of Delaiah, son of Mehetabel, who was confined to his home, he said, Let us meet together in the house of God, within the temple. Let us close the doors of the temple, for they are coming to kill you. They are coming to kill you by night.

The third attack comes in a prophet's voice. Shemaiah is a man shut up in his house, perhaps as a sign, and he speaks with urgency and apparent concern: they are coming for you, tonight; come and hide with me in the holy place, and we will bar the doors. It sounds like a friend saving his life.

But I said, Should such a man as I run away? And what man such as I could go into the temple and live? I will not go in. Two reasons. First, the governor who ran and hid would have told every builder on the wall that the danger was real and the leader was saving himself. Second, Nehemiah was not a priest. The temple building itself was for priests alone, and the law said any outsider who comes near shall be put to death (Num 18:7). A king of Judah had once walked in to burn incense and walked out a leper for the rest of his life (2 Chr 26:16-21). Nehemiah would not buy his safety with a sin.

verseByVerse.quote: And I understood and saw that God had not sent him, but he had pronounced the prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him. For this purpose he was hired, that I should be afraid and act in this way and sin, and so they could give me a bad name in order to taunt me. Remember Tobiah and Sanballat, O my God, according to these things that they did, and also the prophetess Noadiah and the rest of the prophets who wanted to make me afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I understood and saw that God had not sent him, but he had pronounced the prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him. How did he know? Not by some special sense, but because the prophecy told him to break God's law. A word that tells you to sin in order to be safe did not come from God, whoever speaks it and however holy he sounds.

That test is as useful now as then. Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world (1 John 4:1). Counsel that urges you to do what Scripture forbids — to lie a little to protect yourself, to break a vow because the cost has risen, to hide from a duty because someone says God is telling you to — can be answered as Nehemiah answered it: I will not go in.

For this purpose he was hired, that I should be afraid and act in this way and sin, and so they could give me a bad name in order to taunt me. Taunt again, the word the book began with (1:3). They could not bring shame on the wall, so they tried to bring it on the man.

Remember Tobiah and Sanballat, O my God, according to these things that they did, and also the prophetess Noadiah and the rest of the prophets who wanted to make me afraid. So Shemaiah was not alone. There was a prophetess and a group of prophets, all with the same message: be afraid. Nehemiah does not denounce them in public. He hands them to God, as he did at 4:4-5.

verseByVerse.quote: So the wall was finished on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty-two days. And when all our enemies heard of it, all the nations around us were afraid and fell greatly in their own esteem, for they perceived that this work had been accomplished with the help of our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the wall was finished on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty-two days. Elul is August into September. Nehemiah had spoken to the king in Nisan (2:1); five months later, after the long road from Susa and a building season under threat, the wall stood all the way round. Fifty-two days, for a work that had failed for years.

And when all our enemies heard of it, all the nations around us were afraid and fell greatly in their own esteem, for they perceived that this work had been accomplished with the help of our God.

Count the fear in this chapter. The enemies wanted to frighten the builders (v. 9), to make Nehemiah afraid (vv. 13, 14), and Tobiah's letters will still be trying to make him afraid at the end (v. 19). And here, in the middle, it is the nations who are afraid. The fear they manufactured came home to them. The men who laughed at the feeble Jews (4:2) looked at the finished wall and saw God in it.

It is exactly the song of the returned exiles: then they said among the nations, The LORD has done great things for them (Ps 126:2). God does not need his enemies' approval, but he does sometimes make them his witnesses. And the verdict belongs to him. Nehemiah does not say that he had managed a remarkable project. He says the enemies perceived that it had been accomplished with the help of our God, and he lets them say it.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, in those days the nobles of Judah sent many letters to Tobiah, and Tobiah's letters came to them. For many in Judah were bound by oath to him, because he was the son-in-law of Shecaniah the son of Arah: and his son Jehohanan had taken the daughter of Meshullam the son of Berechiah as his wife. Also they spoke of his good deeds in my presence and reported my words to him. And Tobiah sent letters to make me afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book does not stop at the triumph, and that is its honesty. Moreover, in those days the nobles of Judah sent many letters to Tobiah, and Tobiah's letters came to them. While the wall was going up, the nobles were writing to the enemy.

For many in Judah were bound by oath to him, because he was the son-in-law of Shecaniah the son of Arah: and his son Jehohanan had taken the daughter of Meshullam the son of Berechiah as his wife. The sons of Arah were a family of the first return (Ezra 2:5). And Meshullam son of Berechiah had built two sections of this wall with his own hands (3:4, 30). He had built against Tobiah by day and married his daughter into Tobiah's family.

Also they spoke of his good deeds in my presence and reported my words to him. And Tobiah sent letters to make me afraid. Tobiah's friends praised him to Nehemiah's face and carried Nehemiah's words back to him. The wall had closed every gap in the stone, and the enemy walked in through the family.

That is a warning for every work of God. Walls keep out the enemy who attacks; they do nothing against the one you marry into, correspond with, and speak well of. This thread will run to the last chapter, where Tobiah is found living in a room in the temple (13:4-9). The only city whose gates can safely stand open is the one in which nothing unclean will ever enter (Rev 21:27), because its King has dealt with the enemy inside as well as the one outside.

7.overview: The doors are hung, and Nehemiah puts his brother Hanani and the God-fearing Hananiah in charge of Jerusalem, with orders to keep the gates shut till the sun is hot and to set the people as guards before their own homes (vv. 1-3). But the city is large and nearly empty, with no houses rebuilt (v. 4). God puts it into Nehemiah's heart to enrol the people, and he finds the register of those who came up with Zerubbabel ninety years before (v. 5).
