The register follows (vv. 6-73), almost the same as Ezra 2: twelve leaders, the lay families and towns (Bethlehem and Anathoth among them), priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, and those whose descent could not be proved — including priestly families barred until a priest with Urim and Thummim should arise (v. 65). The stated total is 42,360, though the figures sum to 31,089, and many differ from Ezra's copy. The gifts are listed, and the chapter ends as Ezra 2 ends: when the seventh month had come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The City Was Wide and Large
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With the doors hung and gatekeepers, singers and Levites appointed (v. 1), Nehemiah puts his brother Hanani and Hananiah, a more faithful and God-fearing man than many, in charge of Jerusalem, with orders for the gates and the watch (vv. 2-3). The city was wide and large, but the people within it were few, and no houses had been rebuilt (v. 4). Then my God put it into my heart to assemble the nobles and the officials and the people to be enrolled by genealogy, and he finds the register of the first return (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: A wall is not a city. The fifty-two days had produced a perimeter round a place where hardly anyone lived, and the rest of the book is about filling it with a people.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the wall had been built and I had set up the doors, and the gatekeepers, the singers, and the Levites had been appointed, I gave my brother Hanani and Hananiah the governor of the castle charge over Jerusalem, for he was a more faithful and God-fearing man than many. And I said to them, "Let not the gates of Jerusalem be opened until the sun is hot. And while they are still standing guard, let them shut and bar the doors. Appoint guards from among the inhabitants of Jerusalem, some at their guard posts and some in front of their own homes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when the wall had been built and I had set up the doors, and the gatekeepers, the singers, and the Levites had been appointed. The doors are hung at last. And the first appointments are not soldiers but men from the temple: gatekeepers, singers, Levites. The wall was built to guard a place of worship.

I gave my brother Hanani and Hananiah the governor of the castle charge over Jerusalem, for he was a more faithful and God-fearing man than many. Hanani is the brother who brought the news to Susa (1:2). Hananiah, commander of the fortress by the temple, was chosen for his character. Nehemiah does not say he was the most able man, or the best connected. He says he was more faithful and feared God more than most. That is still the first question to ask of anyone given charge of anything in God's house.

Then the orders: the gates stay shut until the sun is hot, well into the morning, when an attack at dawn is no longer possible; they are shut and barred while the guards are still at their posts; and the guards are the city's own people, some in front of their own homes. It is the principle of chapter 3 again. A man watches best the street where his children sleep.

verseByVerse.quote: The city was wide and large, but the people within it were few, and no houses had been rebuilt. Then my God put it into my heart to assemble the nobles and the officials and the people to be enrolled by genealogy. And I found the book of the genealogy of those who came up at the first, and I found written in it:
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city was wide and large, but the people within it were few, and no houses had been rebuilt.

Picture it. A new wall running right round the hills, gates with new doors, and inside, open ground, rubble, a scattering of families, and the temple. The walls had been built for a city that did not yet exist. A church can be like this: a fine building, a well-drawn constitution, and very few people inside who know why they are there.

Then my God put it into my heart to assemble the nobles and the officials and the people to be enrolled by genealogy. It is the phrase he used of the wall itself, what my God had put into my heart (2:12). The idea of a census was as much from God as the idea of a wall. And the first thing he did was look at the past: I found the book of the genealogy of those who came up at the first. Before he decided who should live in Jerusalem, he reminded himself who God had brought home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–60 — Those Who Came Up at the First
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The register of the exiles who came home with Zerubbabel and Jeshua ninety years earlier (vv. 6-7): the lay families (vv. 8-25), the men of the towns, among them Bethlehem and Anathoth (vv. 26-38), the priests (vv. 39-42), the Levites, singers and gatekeepers (vv. 43-45), and the temple servants and sons of Solomon's servants, 392 in all (vv. 46-60).
verseByVerse.theology: It is the same list as Ezra 2, copied a second time, and the repetition is the point: Nehemiah's people are the people God brought home. But a good many of the numbers differ between the two copies, and the differences are reported below rather than hidden.

verseByVerse.quote: These were the people of the province who came up out of the captivity of those exiles whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried into exile. They returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his town. They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum, Baanah. The number of the men of the people of Israel:
verseByVerse.commentary:
These were the people of the province who came up out of the captivity of those exiles whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried into exile. They returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his town. What follows is the register of the first return, under Cyrus, some ninety years before. It is the list already given in Ezra 2, copied into this book almost entire.

They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum, Baanah. Twelve leaders; Ezra's copy names eleven. Twelve is the number of the tribes, and it says that this small company was all Israel in miniature. The Nehemiah and Mordecai in the list are other men of the same names, who came home ninety years before the governor who is telling this story.

verseByVerse.quote: the sons of Parosh, 2,172. The sons of Shephatiah, 372. The sons of Arah, 652. The sons of Pahath-moab, namely the sons of Jeshua and Joab, 2,818. The sons of Elam, 1,254. The sons of Zattu, 845. The sons of Zaccai, 760. The sons of Binnui, 648. The sons of Bebai, 628. The sons of Azgad, 2,322. The sons of Adonikam, 667. The sons of Bigvai, 2,067. The sons of Adin, 655. The sons of Ater, namely of Hezekiah, 98. The sons of Hashum, 328. The sons of Bezai, 324. The sons of Hariph, 112. The sons of Gibeon, 95.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the families: the sons of Parosh, 2,172, and on through eighteen lines of names and numbers. Most of these people appear nowhere else in the Bible. They are here because they left Babylon, where most Jews stayed, for a ruined country and an uncertain welcome, on the strength of a promise.

A word on the numbers, since a careful reader will compare this chapter with Ezra 2 and find that many of them differ. The family of Adonikam is 666 in Ezra and 667 here; Azgad is 1,222 there and 2,322 here. Numbers are the easiest thing in any manuscript to miscopy, and these are two copies of one list made by hand. Nothing in the faith hangs on the size of the family of Azgad. What the list is for does not change: God brought these people home.

The last line of the section is the sons of Gibeon, 95. Hold that name for a moment, because the towns that follow finish the thought.

verseByVerse.quote: The men of Bethlehem and Netophah, 188. The men of Anathoth, 128. The men of Beth-azmaveth, 42. The men of Kiriath-jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth, 743. The men of Ramah and Geba, 621. The men of Michmas, 122. The men of Bethel and Ai, 123. The men of the other Nebo, 52. The sons of the other Elam, 1,254. The sons of Harim, 320. The sons of Jericho, 345. The sons of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, 721. The sons of Senaah, 3,930.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From here the list runs by towns, and the towns have histories. The men of Bethlehem and Netophah, 188 (v. 26): the town of David, of which Micah had said, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel (Mic 5:2). Some of those 188 were among the forebears of the families still living there when Joseph also went up from Galilee ... to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem (Luke 2:4). The Ruler was born in a town that had been emptied and then resettled by people on this list.

The men of Anathoth, 128 (v. 27). Anathoth was Jeremiah's town. With the Babylonian army outside Jerusalem, he had bought a field there, on God's word, as a sign that houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land (Jer 32:15). Here are 128 men of Anathoth, home again, on land that a prophet had paid for in a siege.

The men of Kiriath-jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth, 743 (v. 29). Put those beside Gibeon in verse 25 and you have the four cities of the Gibeonites, the Canaanites who deceived Joshua and were spared: their cities were Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath-jearim (Josh 9:17). Their descendants went into exile with Judah and came home with Judah, and in chapter 3 the men of Gibeon built a stretch of the wall. Kiriath-jearim is also where the ark stayed for twenty years before David brought it up to Jerusalem (1 Sam 7:1-2). The people who had once been the outsiders had become the keepers of the ark.

Then Michmas, where Jonathan and his armour-bearer climbed the cliff (1 Sam 14); Bethel and Ai, the place of Jacob's ladder and the place of Israel's first defeat, in one line (v. 32); Jericho, whose men built beside the high priest (3:2); and Lod, Hadid, and Ono (v. 37). Ono is the plain where Sanballat tried to lure Nehemiah (6:2). There were Jewish families living there, which is perhaps why the invitation sounded reasonable.

verseByVerse.quote: The priests: the sons of Jedaiah, namely the house of Jeshua, 973. The sons of Immer, 1,052. The sons of Pashhur, 1,247. The sons of Harim, 1,017.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests: the sons of Jedaiah, namely the house of Jeshua, 973. The sons of Immer, 1,052. The sons of Pashhur, 1,247. The sons of Harim, 1,017.

Four priestly families, 4,289 men. Add them up and set them against the next verse: the Levites, who assisted the priests, number seventy-four. The priests had a great deal to come home to, and the Levites, whose work was the carrying and serving, had not come. When Ezra brought his own company, eighty years later, he had to send back specially for Levites because he found none (Ezra 8:15).

verseByVerse.quote: The Levites: the sons of Jeshua, namely of Kadmiel of the sons of Hodevah, 74. The singers: the sons of Asaph, 148. The gatekeepers: the sons of Shallum, the sons of Ater, the sons of Talmon, the sons of Akkub, the sons of Hatita, the sons of Shobai, 138. The temple servants: the sons of Ziha, the sons of Hasupha, the sons of Tabbaoth, the sons of Keros, the sons of Sia, the sons of Padon, the sons of Lebana, the sons of Hagaba, the sons of Shalmai, the sons of Hanan, the sons of Giddel, the sons of Gahar, the sons of Reaiah, the sons of Rezin, the sons of Nekoda, the sons of Gazzam, the sons of Uzza, the sons of Paseah, the sons of Besai, the sons of Meunim, the sons of Nephushesim, the sons of Bakbuk, the sons of Hakupha, the sons of Harhur, the sons of Bazlith, the sons of Mehida, the sons of Harsha, the sons of Barkos, the sons of Sisera, the sons of Temah, the sons of Neziah, the sons of Hatipha. The sons of Solomon's servants: the sons of Sotai, the sons of Sophereth, the sons of Perida, the sons of Jaala, the sons of Darkon, the sons of Giddel, the sons of Shephatiah, the sons of Hattil, the sons of Pochereth-hazzebaim, the sons of Amon. All the temple servants and the sons of Solomon's servants were 392.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites ... 74. The singers: the sons of Asaph, 148. The gatekeepers ... 138. The singers are the descendants of Asaph, David's chief musician; ninety years after the return they are still singing his psalms in the rebuilt temple, and Nehemiah has just appointed them again (v. 1).

Then two groups of families with no numbers of their own: the temple servants and the sons of Solomon's servants, 392 between them (v. 60). They were probably descended from foreigners given to the work of the temple long before — Ezra calls them the temple servants, whom David and his officials had set apart to attend the Levites (Ezra 8:20). Families who began as outsiders and servants are listed in the register of God's people, name after name, alongside the priests.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 61–73 — Until a Priest Should Arise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some families could not prove that they belonged to Israel, and three priestly families could not find their names in the genealogies and were excluded from the priesthood as unclean (vv. 61-64), until a priest with Urim and Thummim should arise (v. 65). The whole assembly was 42,360, with servants, singers and animals (vv. 66-69). The governor, the heads of families and the people gave gold, silver and priests' garments (vv. 70-72). And when the seventh month had come, the people of Israel were in their towns (v. 73).
verseByVerse.theology: The register ends on an open question about who is a priest, and on a date. Ezra 2 ends with the same sentence, and in both books what follows is the people gathering in Jerusalem as one man.

verseByVerse.quote: The following were those who came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer, but they could not prove their fathers' houses nor their descent, whether they belonged to Israel: the sons of Delaiah, the sons of Tobiah, the sons of Nekoda, 642. Also, of the priests: the sons of Hobaiah, the sons of Hakkoz, the sons of Barzillai (who had taken a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite and was called by their name). These sought their registration among those enrolled in the genealogies, but it was not found there, so they were excluded from the priesthood as unclean. The governor told them that they were not to partake of the most holy food until a priest with Urim and Thummim should arise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the hard part of the list. Some came home but they could not prove their fathers' houses nor their descent, whether they belonged to Israel: 642 people of three families (vv. 61-62). They are not sent away. They are simply recorded as unproven.

And three families of priests — the sons of Hobaiah, the sons of Hakkoz, the sons of Barzillai — searched for their names in the records and it was not found there, so they were excluded from the priesthood as unclean. The governor told them that they were not to partake of the most holy food until a priest with Urim and Thummim should arise. The Urim and Thummim were the means by which the high priest had once received God's answer to a question. There was no one who could use them. So the question was left open, waiting for God.

The third of those families has a sad little story in its bracket. A priest had married a daughter of Barzillai the Gileadite, the wealthy old man who fed David in his flight from Absalom (2 Sam 19:31-32), and he was called by their name. He took the famous name of his wife's family, and his descendants lost the name that made them priests. It is possible to gain a distinguished name and lose a birthright.

Remember Hakkoz. In chapter 3 a man called Meremoth the son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz built two sections of the wall (3:4, 21), and Ezra calls him Meremoth the priest (Ezra 8:33). Somewhere in those ninety years the family that could not find its name was found. Whatever settled it, God had not forgotten them.

And one Priest did arise who could not have passed this test either. It is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah, and in connection with that tribe Moses said nothing about priests (Heb 7:14). He had no priestly genealogy to produce. He has become a priest, not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent, but by the power of an indestructible life (Heb 7:16). Everyone who cannot prove his place before God can have it through him.

verseByVerse.quote: The whole assembly together was 42,360, besides their male and female servants, of whom there were 7,337. And they had 245 singers, male and female. Their horses were 736, their mules 245, their camels 435, and their donkeys 6,720.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole assembly together was 42,360, besides their male and female servants, of whom there were 7,337. And they had 245 singers, male and female. Then the animals: 736 horses, 245 mules, 435 camels, 6,720 donkeys.

Do the arithmetic and something does not add up. The family and town figures in this chapter (vv. 8-62) total 31,089, and the stated total is 42,360, so 11,271 people are unaccounted for. Ezra's copy has the same total, and its figures come to 29,818. Perhaps the total counts people the family lists do not, such as members of other tribes or families not listed by name; perhaps the difference lies in the copying. The honest answer is that we do not know. The singers, too, are 245 here and 200 in Ezra. None of this is hidden, and none of it touches the point: tens of thousands came home, with their servants and their donkeys, because God had said they would.

verseByVerse.quote: Now some of the heads of fathers' houses gave to the work. The governor gave to the treasury 1,000 darics of gold, 50 basins, 30 priests' garments and 500 minas of silver. And some of the heads of fathers' houses gave into the treasury of the work 20,000 darics of gold and 2,200 minas of silver. And what the rest of the people gave was 20,000 darics of gold, 2,000 minas of silver, and 67 priests' garments. So the priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, the singers, some of the people, the temple servants, and all Israel, lived in their towns. And when the seventh month had come, the people of Israel were in their towns.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now some of the heads of fathers' houses gave to the work. The governor gave to the treasury 1,000 darics of gold, 50 basins, 30 priests' garments and 500 minas of silver. The governor here is the governor of the first return, because this is still the old register; it is not Nehemiah's own gift. The heads of families gave 20,000 darics and 2,200 minas, and the rest of the people 20,000 darics, 2,000 minas and 67 garments.

Ezra's copy gives round totals: 61,000 darics, 5,000 minas and 100 garments (Ezra 2:69). Add Nehemiah's itemized gifts and the silver comes to 4,700 minas and the garments to 97, close to Ezra's round figures; the gold comes to 41,000. And notice the rest of the people. The ordinary families gave as much gold as the heads of houses.

So the priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, the singers, some of the people, the temple servants, and all Israel, lived in their towns. And when the seventh month had come, the people of Israel were in their towns.

That last sentence is also the opening of Ezra 3: When the seventh month came, and the children of Israel were in the towns, the people gathered as one man to Jerusalem (Ezra 3:1). Ninety years earlier the list ended, the seventh month came, and the people gathered as one man to build an altar. Now the list ends, the seventh month comes, and the next verse says all the people gathered as one man (8:1). This time they ask for a book. The sacrifice first, then the Word: God had given them both, and the city was about to be filled with the second.

7.theology:
A wall does not make a city; a people does. Nehemiah defines the people of the rebuilt city by the people God had brought home, and the list of ordinary families is itself a record of God's faithfulness to his promise to gather (1:9).

The register leaves open who is a priest, until a priest should arise who could answer for God. Christ is that Priest — and he had no priestly genealogy at all, being of Judah; he is priest by the power of an indestructible life (Heb 7:14-16), and through him those who cannot prove their place before God are given it.
7.examples:
A new wall round an empty city.

Hananiah was chosen because he feared God more than most.

The Nehemiah and Mordecai in the list are other men, ninety years earlier.

188 men of Bethlehem came home; the Ruler would be born there.

128 men of Anathoth came home to land a prophet had bought during the siege.

4,289 priests and 74 Levites.

The figures add up to 31,089; the total says 42,360. The text does not hide it.

The family of Hakkoz, barred for want of a genealogy, later produced a priest who built two sections of the wall.

8.title: The Open Book
8.text: <sup>1</sup>And all the people gathered as one man into the square before the Water Gate. And they told Ezra the scribe to bring the Book of the Law of Moses that the LORD had commanded Israel.<sup>2</sup>So Ezra the priest brought the Law before the assembly, both men and women and all who could understand what they heard, on the first day of the seventh month.<sup>3</sup>And he read from it facing the square before the Water Gate from early morning until midday, in the presence of the men and the women and those who could understand. And the ears of all the people were attentive to the Book of the Law.<sup>4</sup>And Ezra the scribe stood on a wooden platform that they had made for the purpose. And beside him stood Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah, and Maaseiah on his right hand, and Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchijah, Hashum, Hashbaddanah, Zechariah, and Meshullam on his left hand.<sup>5</sup>And Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people, for he was above all the people, and as he opened it all the people stood.<sup>6</sup>And Ezra blessed the LORD, the great God, and all the people answered, "Amen, Amen," lifting up their hands. And they bowed their heads and worshiped the LORD with their faces to the ground.<sup>7</sup>Also Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodiah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah, the Levites, helped the people to understand the Law, while the people remained in their places.<sup>8</sup>They read from the book, from the Law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading.<sup>9</sup>And Nehemiah, who was the governor, and Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who taught the people said to all the people, "This day is holy to the LORD your God; do not mourn or weep." For all the people wept as they heard the words of the Law.<sup>10</sup>Then he said to them, "Go your way. Eat the fat and drink sweet wine and send portions to anyone who has nothing ready, for this day is holy to our Lord. And do not be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength."<sup>11</sup>So the Levites calmed all the people, saying, "Be quiet, for this day is holy; do not be grieved."<sup>12</sup>And all the people went their way to eat and drink and to send portions and to make great rejoicing, because they had understood the words that were declared to them.<sup>13</sup>On the second day the heads of fathers' houses of all the people, with the priests and the Levites, came together to Ezra the scribe in order to study the words of the Law.<sup>14</sup>And they found it written in the Law that the LORD had commanded by Moses that the people of Israel should dwell in booths during the feast of the seventh month,<sup>15</sup>and that they should proclaim it and publish it in all their towns and in Jerusalem, "Go out to the hills and bring branches of olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm, and other leafy trees to make booths, as it is written."<sup>16</sup>So the people went out and brought them and made booths for themselves, each on his roof, and in their courts and in the courts of the house of God, and in the square at the Water Gate and in the square at the Gate of Ephraim.<sup>17</sup>And all the assembly of those who had returned from the captivity made booths and lived in the booths, for from the days of Jeshua the son of Nun to that day the people of Israel had not done so. And there was very great rejoicing.<sup>18</sup>And day by day, from the first day to the last day, he read from the Book of the Law of God. They kept the feast seven days, and on the eighth day there was a solemn assembly, according to the rule.
8.overview: On the first day of the seventh month the whole people gather as one man at the Water Gate and ask Ezra to bring the Book of the Law. He reads from dawn to midday from a wooden platform to men, women and all who can understand; the people stand, answer Amen, Amen, and bow to the ground, while the Levites move among them explaining, so that the people understood the reading (vv. 1-8). They weep as they hear the law, but Nehemiah the governor, Ezra and the Levites declare the day holy: go and feast, send portions to those who have nothing, for the joy of the LORD is your strength — and the people rejoice because they had understood (vv. 9-12). On the second day the leaders study the law and find the command to live in booths; the whole community builds booths on roofs, courtyards and squares, as had not been done in that way since Joshua, with very great rejoicing, and the law is read every day of the feast (vv. 13-18).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the first day of the seventh month all the people gather as one man into the square before the Water Gate and ask Ezra to bring the Book of the Law (vv. 1-2). He reads from early morning until midday to men, women and all who could understand, and the ears of all the people were attentive to the Book of the Law (v. 3). He stands on a wooden platform, opens the book, and the people stand; he blesses the LORD, and they answer Amen, Amen with hands raised and faces to the ground (vv. 4-6). The Levites help the people understand: They read from the book, from the Law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: The walls were finished to protect this: a people gathered round God's Word, wanting it, standing for it, and having it made plain.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the people gathered as one man into the square before the Water Gate. And they told Ezra the scribe to bring the Book of the Law of Moses that the LORD had commanded Israel. So Ezra the priest brought the Law before the assembly, both men and women and all who could understand what they heard, on the first day of the seventh month.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all the people gathered as one man into the square before the Water Gate. And they told Ezra the scribe to bring the Book of the Law of Moses that the LORD had commanded Israel.

As one man. Ninety years before, when the first exiles had come home, the seventh month came and the people gathered as one man to Jerusalem to build an altar (Ezra 3:1). Now the wall is up, the seventh month has come again (7:73), and they gather as one man in the square by the Water Gate, below the temple, where the temple servants had built their stretch of wall (3:26). And the striking thing is who asks. It is not Nehemiah calling a meeting, or Ezra announcing a lecture. They told Ezra the scribe to bring the Book. The people wanted to hear it.

So Ezra the priest brought the Law before the assembly, both men and women and all who could understand what they heard, on the first day of the seventh month. Men and women, and every child old enough to follow. Moses had commanded this very scene: Assemble the people, men, women, and little ones, and the sojourner within your towns, that they may hear and learn to fear the LORD your God (Deut 31:12). And the first day of the seventh month was a holy day already, a memorial proclaimed with blast of trumpets, a holy convocation (Lev 23:24). The trumpets had called them together. The book told them why.

verseByVerse.quote: And he read from it facing the square before the Water Gate from early morning until midday, in the presence of the men and the women and those who could understand. And the ears of all the people were attentive to the Book of the Law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he read from it facing the square before the Water Gate from early morning until midday, in the presence of the men and the women and those who could understand. And the ears of all the people were attentive to the Book of the Law.

From first light to noon: five or six hours, standing in an open square as the sun climbed. That is the length of a working day spent listening to Scripture. And they listened. The ears of all the people were attentive.

Put that beside Nehemiah's first prayer. In Susa he had asked God, let your ear be attentive ... to hear the prayer of your servant (1:6). God had heard, and the wall was the proof. Now, in the finished city, the direction is reversed, and the people's ears are attentive to God. That is what the whole building project was for.

A question to put to ourselves: how long could we listen? Not to a sermon about Scripture, but to Scripture itself. These people had been without a clear reading of the law for most of their lives, and they were hungry for it. We have it in our own language on the table beside the bed, and hunger is the thing we most often lack.

verseByVerse.quote: And Ezra the scribe stood on a wooden platform that they had made for the purpose. And beside him stood Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah, and Maaseiah on his right hand, and Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchijah, Hashum, Hashbaddanah, Zechariah, and Meshullam on his left hand. And Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people, for he was above all the people, and as he opened it all the people stood. And Ezra blessed the LORD, the great God, and all the people answered, "Amen, Amen," lifting up their hands. And they bowed their heads and worshiped the LORD with their faces to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Ezra the scribe stood on a wooden platform that they had made for the purpose. The word is literally a tower: a raised wooden stand, built for the day, so that a crowd filling a city square could see and hear him. Thirteen men stood with him, six on his right and seven on his left, leaders of the people standing with the reader, not in front of him.

And Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people, for he was above all the people, and as he opened it all the people stood. The book was a scroll, unrolled in front of them, and as it opened the whole square rose to its feet. Nobody had to tell them to. They stood because God was about to speak. Centuries later, in a small synagogue in Nazareth, a man stood up to read, unrolled the scroll of Isaiah, and then said, Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing (Luke 4:16, 21).

And Ezra blessed the LORD, the great God, and all the people answered, Amen, Amen, lifting up their hands. And they bowed their heads and worshiped the LORD with their faces to the ground. Amen means it is true, let it be so. They said it twice, with their hands up, and then went down on their faces. Before a word of the law had been read, they had agreed with it and bowed to it. That is the posture in which Scripture is rightly heard.

And Ezra's blessing named him the great God, the title Nehemiah had prayed to in Susa (1:5) and shouted to the builders on the wall (4:14). The God who had been great enough to turn a king and finish a wall was now great enough to speak.

verseByVerse.quote: Also Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodiah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah, the Levites, helped the people to understand the Law, while the people remained in their places. They read from the book, from the Law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Also Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah ... the Levites, helped the people to understand the Law, while the people remained in their places. Thirteen Levites move among the crowd as Ezra reads. The people stay where they are; the teachers come to them.

They read from the book, from the Law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading.

This one sentence describes what preaching is for. Three things. They read the text itself, the Law of God, not something about it. They read it clearly; the word means distinctly, and many think it included putting the Hebrew into Aramaic, the everyday language most of these people had grown up with in exile. And they gave the sense: they explained it, so that the meaning got through. The test was not whether the teachers had been impressive. It was so that the people understood.

The greatest Teacher did exactly this. On the road to Emmaus, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself; and afterwards he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:27, 45). The Levites could explain the law. Only Christ could open the mind that hears it, and he still does.

Some of these names will be heard again. Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah and Hodiah are among the Levites who stand on the stairs in the next chapter and lead the people in confessing their sins (9:4-5). The men who explained the law are the men who lead the prayer it produced. Teaching that is understood turns into prayer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–12 — The Joy of the LORD Is Your Strength
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people weep as they hear the law. Nehemiah the governor, Ezra and the Levites tell them, This day is holy to the LORD your God; do not mourn or weep (v. 9). Go your way. Eat the fat and drink sweet wine and send portions to anyone who has nothing ready, for this day is holy to our Lord. And do not be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength (v. 10). The Levites quiet them (v. 11), and they go home to make great rejoicing, because they had understood the words that were declared to them (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Strength is the Hebrew word for a stronghold. A week after the wall was finished, Nehemiah tells them that their real fortress is the joy of the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: And Nehemiah, who was the governor, and Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who taught the people said to all the people, "This day is holy to the LORD your God; do not mourn or weep." For all the people wept as they heard the words of the Law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Nehemiah, who was the governor, and Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who taught the people said to all the people, This day is holy to the LORD your God; do not mourn or weep. For all the people wept as they heard the words of the Law.

They wept. Not because the reading was long, and not because it was dull. They wept because they understood it. They heard what God had commanded, and they knew their fathers had not done it, and neither had they. Commands about the Sabbath, about marriage, about the poor; blessings promised for obedience and curses for disobedience, and they were standing in the ruins the curses had made. The law had done what it is for: through the law comes knowledge of sin (Rom 3:20).

Nehemiah is named here beside Ezra, the governor and the priest and scribe, the builder of the wall and the teacher of the law standing together, one of the few places in the book where the two men appear side by side (8:9; 12:26, 36). And their first word to a weeping crowd is not that they should weep more. It is this day is holy to the LORD your God. It was a feast day, and God had not called them together to grieve.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to them, "Go your way. Eat the fat and drink sweet wine and send portions to anyone who has nothing ready, for this day is holy to our Lord. And do not be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he said to them, Go your way. Eat the fat and drink sweet wine and send portions to anyone who has nothing ready, for this day is holy to our Lord. And do not be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.

Go home and have a feast. The best cuts of meat, sweet wine, and send some to anyone who has nothing, so no one in the city is left out of the celebration. It is the same custom, in the same words in Hebrew, that Esther records for Purim: days for sending gifts of food to one another and gifts to the poor (Esth 9:22). God's holy days are feasts, and feasts are shared.

The joy of the LORD is your strength. The word for strength is the word for a stronghold, a fortress — the word of the LORD is the stronghold of my life; of whom shall I be afraid? (Ps 27:1). They had spent fifty-two days building a wall with swords at their sides. A few days later Nehemiah tells them where their real fortress is. It is not the wall. It is the joy of the LORD.

Whose joy? The words can mean joy in the LORD, the gladness of people who know him; and they can mean the LORD's own joy, his delight over his people. Scripture gives us both. He will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing (Zeph 3:17). The people standing in that square, weeping over broken commands, were the people God was singing over. Their tears were right. But the fortress that would hold them was not how sorry they were. It was how glad he was to have them back.

That is still the order. Anyone who has seen his own sin clearly knows the weeping. The joy that holds a Christian up is not a feeling he generates; it is the Father's joy over a son come home (Luke 15:24), and it was bought by the One who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross (Heb 12:2).

verseByVerse.quote: So the Levites calmed all the people, saying, "Be quiet, for this day is holy; do not be grieved." And all the people went their way to eat and drink and to send portions and to make great rejoicing, because they had understood the words that were declared to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the Levites calmed all the people, saying, Be quiet, for this day is holy; do not be grieved. Picture the Levites going through the crowd as they had during the reading, now with a different message: hush, this is a holy day, stop grieving. The same men who explained the law explained that it was a feast.

And all the people went their way to eat and drink and to send portions and to make great rejoicing, because they had understood the words that were declared to them.

Because they had understood. The same understanding that made them weep in the morning made them rejoice in the afternoon. Nothing new had been read. What had changed was that they understood not only what God required but what kind of God had given it and called them to a feast in spite of all they had failed to do. Joy that does not come from understanding does not last. This did.

The two disciples on the Emmaus road knew the same thing: Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures? (Luke 24:32). And the Gospel ends with the disciples going back to Jerusalem with great joy (Luke 24:52). Understood Scripture, opened by the Lord, ends in joy.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the second day the leaders return to study the law and find the command to live in booths during the feast of the seventh month (vv. 13-15). The people build booths on roofs, in courtyards, in the temple courts and the city squares (v. 16). For from the days of Jeshua the son of Nun to that day the people of Israel had not done so. And there was very great rejoicing (v. 17). Ezra reads the law every day of the feast, and on the eighth day there is a solemn assembly (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: Booths remembered the wilderness, when God's people lived in tents and God lived among them in his. It was at this feast, on its last great day, that Jesus stood up in the temple and cried, If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37).

verseByVerse.quote: On the second day the heads of fathers' houses of all the people, with the priests and the Levites, came together to Ezra the scribe in order to study the words of the Law. And they found it written in the Law that the LORD had commanded by Moses that the people of Israel should dwell in booths during the feast of the seventh month, and that they should proclaim it and publish it in all their towns and in Jerusalem, "Go out to the hills and bring branches of olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm, and other leafy trees to make booths, as it is written."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the second day the heads of fathers' houses of all the people, with the priests and the Levites, came together to Ezra the scribe in order to study the words of the Law. The next morning the leaders are back. Having heard it once, they want to understand it better, so that they can lead their households in it. That is how you tell a real hearing of God's Word from an emotional one: the next day you want more of it.

And they found it written in the Law that the LORD had commanded by Moses that the people of Israel should dwell in booths during the feast of the seventh month. The Feast of Booths began on the fifteenth of this month, only two weeks away (Lev 23:34), and the law said You shall dwell in booths for seven days ... that your generations may know that I made the people of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt (Lev 23:42-43). So word went out to every town: Go out to the hills and bring branches of olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm, and other leafy trees to make booths, as it is written.

verseByVerse.quote: So the people went out and brought them and made booths for themselves, each on his roof, and in their courts and in the courts of the house of God, and in the square at the Water Gate and in the square at the Gate of Ephraim. And all the assembly of those who had returned from the captivity made booths and lived in the booths, for from the days of Jeshua the son of Nun to that day the people of Israel had not done so. And there was very great rejoicing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the people went out and brought them and made booths for themselves, each on his roof, and in their courts and in the courts of the house of God, and in the square at the Water Gate and in the square at the Gate of Ephraim. Imagine the city that week. Flat roofs covered with shelters of green branches, courtyards full of them, the temple courts, the squares by the gates. The empty city of 7:4 had filled with people living outdoors under leaves.

And all the assembly of those who had returned from the captivity made booths and lived in the booths, for from the days of Jeshua the son of Nun to that day the people of Israel had not done so. And there was very great rejoicing.

That sentence needs care, because the feast itself had been kept. Solomon kept it (2 Chr 8:13), and the first returnees kept it ninety years before: they kept the Feast of Booths, as it is written (Ezra 3:4). What had not happened since Joshua was this: the whole assembly, every household, actually living in booths for the week, as the law commanded. Many had kept the sacrifices of the feast. Not since the conquest had the people as a whole done it in the way God had described.

Look too at the name in that sentence. Jeshua is the same name as Joshua, and in Greek it is Jesus. The first Joshua brought the people into the land, but he did not bring them into God's final rest: if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on (Heb 4:8). These returned exiles in their booths were still pilgrims, as their fathers had been in the wilderness. Their rest was still to come, with a greater Jeshua.

verseByVerse.quote: And day by day, from the first day to the last day, he read from the Book of the Law of God. They kept the feast seven days, and on the eighth day there was a solemn assembly, according to the rule.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And day by day, from the first day to the last day, he read from the Book of the Law of God. They kept the feast seven days, and on the eighth day there was a solemn assembly, according to the rule.

Every day of the feast the book was read. That is Moses' command kept to the letter: at the Feast of Booths ... you shall read this law before all Israel in their hearing (Deut 31:10-11). A week of living in the open, eating together, and hearing God's Word each day, and then the eighth day, the great closing assembly.

Five centuries later, at this same feast, on this same last day, the Word himself stood in the temple courts. On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water (John 7:37-38). The people in their booths remembered that God had once lived among them in a tent. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14) — the word John uses means pitched his tent. The feast of booths was waiting for him.

8.theology:
The wall was built to protect this: a people gathered round the Word of God, read and made plain. The Word first shows them their sin, and they weep; then it declares the day holy and sends them to feast. Law and gospel, grief and joy, in the right order.

The joy of the LORD is your strength: their stronghold was not the wall but the joy of a God who rejoices over his people (Zeph 3:17). Christ opens the Scriptures so that hearts burn (Luke 24:32), endured the cross for the joy set before him (Heb 12:2), and stood up on the last day of this very feast to offer living water to anyone who thirsts (John 7:37-38).
8.examples:
The people asked for the book.

They listened from first light to noon.

When the scroll opened, the whole square stood up.

They said Amen, Amen before the reading began.

The Levites read clearly and gave the sense, so that people understood.

They wept because they understood; they rejoiced because they understood.

A week after the wall, Nehemiah said their fortress was the joy of the LORD.

The city's roofs were covered with booths of branches.

9.title: The God Who Never Gave Up
9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now on the twenty-fourth day of this month the people of Israel were assembled with fasting and in sackcloth, and with earth on their heads.<sup>2</sup>And the Israelites separated themselves from all foreigners and stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers.<sup>3</sup>And they stood up in their place and read from the Book of the Law of the LORD their God for a quarter of the day; for another quarter of it they made confession and worshiped the LORD their God.<sup>4</sup>On the stairs of the Levites stood Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani; and they cried with a loud voice to the LORD their God.<sup>5</sup>Then the Levites, Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabneiah, Sherebiah, Hodiah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, "Stand up and bless the LORD your God from everlasting to everlasting. Blessed be your glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise.<sup>6</sup>"You are the LORD, you alone. You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their host, the earth and all that is on it, the seas and all that is in them; and you preserve all of them; and the host of heaven worships you.<sup>7</sup>You are the LORD, the God who chose Abram and brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans and gave him the name Abraham.<sup>8</sup>You found his heart faithful before you, and made with him the covenant to give to his offspring the land of the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Jebusite, and the Girgashite. And you have kept your promise, for you are righteous.<sup>9</sup>"And you saw the affliction of our fathers in Egypt and heard their cry at the Red Sea,<sup>10</sup>and performed signs and wonders against Pharaoh and all his servants and all the people of his land, for you knew that they acted arrogantly against our fathers. And you made a name for yourself, as it is to this day.<sup>11</sup>And you divided the sea before them, so that they went through the midst of the sea on dry land, and you cast their pursuers into the depths, as a stone into mighty waters.<sup>12</sup>By a pillar of cloud you led them in the day, and by a pillar of fire in the night to light for them the way in which they should go.<sup>13</sup>You came down on Mount Sinai and spoke with them from heaven and gave them right rules and true laws, good statutes and commandments,<sup>14</sup>and you made known to them your holy Sabbath and commanded them commandments and statutes and a law by Moses your servant.<sup>15</sup>You gave them bread from heaven for their hunger and brought water for them out of the rock for their thirst, and you told them to go in to possess the land that you had sworn to give them.<sup>16</sup>"But they and our fathers acted presumptuously and stiffened their neck and did not obey your commandments.<sup>17</sup>They refused to obey and were not mindful of the wonders that you performed among them, but they stiffened their neck and appointed a leader to return to their slavery in Egypt. But you are a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and did not forsake them.<sup>18</sup>Even when they had made for themselves a golden calf and said, 'This is your God who brought you up out of Egypt,' and had committed great blasphemies,<sup>19</sup>you in your great mercies did not forsake them in the wilderness. The pillar of cloud to lead them in the way did not depart from them by day, nor the pillar of fire by night to light for them the way by which they should go.<sup>20</sup>You gave your good Spirit to instruct them and did not withhold your manna from their mouth and gave them water for their thirst.<sup>21</sup>Forty years you sustained them in the wilderness, and they lacked nothing. Their clothes did not wear out and their feet did not swell.<sup>22</sup>"And you gave them kingdoms and peoples and allotted to them every corner. So they took possession of the land of Sihon king of Heshbon and the land of Og king of Bashan.<sup>23</sup>You multiplied their children as the stars of heaven, and you brought them into the land that you had told their fathers to enter and possess.<sup>24</sup>So the descendants went in and possessed the land, and you subdued before them the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, and gave them into their hand, with their kings and the peoples of the land, that they might do with them as they would.<sup>25</sup>And they captured fortified cities and a rich land, and took possession of houses full of all good things, cisterns already hewn, vineyards, olive orchards and fruit trees in abundance. So they ate and were filled and became fat and delighted themselves in your great goodness.<sup>26</sup>"Nevertheless, they were disobedient and rebelled against you and cast your law behind their back and killed your prophets, who had warned them in order to turn them back to you, and they committed great blasphemies.<sup>27</sup>Therefore you gave them into the hand of their enemies, who made them suffer. And in the time of their suffering they cried out to you and you heard them from heaven, and according to your great mercies you gave them saviors who saved them from the hand of their enemies.<sup>28</sup>But after they had rest they did evil again before you, and you abandoned them to the hand of their enemies, so that they had dominion over them. Yet when they turned and cried to you, you heard from heaven, and many times you delivered them according to your mercies.<sup>29</sup>And you warned them in order to turn them back to your law. Yet they acted presumptuously and did not obey your commandments, but sinned against your rules, which if a person does them, he shall live by them, and they turned a stubborn shoulder and stiffened their neck and would not obey.<sup>30</sup>Many years you bore with them and warned them by your Spirit through your prophets. Yet they would not give ear. Therefore you gave them into the hand of the peoples of the lands.<sup>31</sup>Nevertheless, in your great mercies you did not make an end of them or forsake them, for you are a gracious and merciful God.<sup>32</sup>"Now, therefore, our God, the great, the mighty, and the awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love, let not all the hardship seem little to you that has come upon us, upon our kings, our princes, our priests, our prophets, our fathers, and all your people, since the time of the kings of Assyria until this day.<sup>33</sup>Yet you have been righteous in all that has come upon us, for you have dealt faithfully and we have acted wickedly.<sup>34</sup>Our kings, our princes, our priests, and our fathers have not kept your law or paid attention to your commandments and your warnings that you gave them.<sup>35</sup>Even in their own kingdom, and amid your great goodness that you gave them, and in the large and rich land that you set before them, they did not serve you or turn from their wicked works.<sup>36</sup>Behold, we are slaves this day; in the land that you gave to our fathers to enjoy its fruit and its good gifts, behold, we are slaves.<sup>37</sup>And its rich yield goes to the kings whom you have set over us because of our sins. They rule over our bodies and over our livestock as they please, and we are in great distress.<sup>38</sup>"Because of all this we make a firm covenant in writing; on the sealed document are the names of our princes, our Levites, and our priests.
9.overview: Two days after Booths the people gather in fasting and sackcloth, separate themselves, read the law for a quarter of the day and confess for another (vv. 1-3). The Levites call them to stand and bless God (vv. 4-5), and the great prayer tells Israel's whole history as the history of God: the only Creator (v. 6); the God who chose Abraham and kept his promise, for you are righteous (vv. 7-8); the Exodus, Sinai, manna and water (vv. 9-15). Then Israel's rebellion, answered each time by a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful — after the calf, in the wilderness, in the land, through the judges and the prophets they killed — until you did not make an end of them or forsake them (vv. 16-31). It closes on the present: God has been righteous in all of it; behold, we are slaves this day in the land given to their fathers, and we are in great distress (vv. 32-37). So they make a firm covenant in writing and seal it (v. 38).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Stand Up and Bless the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the twenty-fourth day of the month the people assemble with fasting, sackcloth and earth on their heads, separate themselves from foreigners, and confess their sins and the iniquities of their fathers (vv. 1-2). For a quarter of the day they read the law and for another quarter they confess and worship (v. 3). The Levites cry out from the stairs and call the people: Stand up and bless the LORD your God from everlasting to everlasting. Blessed be your glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The fasting came after the feasting, not before. They had been told first that the joy of the LORD was their strength (8:10), and only then did they sit in sackcloth. Confession made by people who already know they are loved can go all the way down.

verseByVerse.quote: Now on the twenty-fourth day of this month the people of Israel were assembled with fasting and in sackcloth, and with earth on their heads. And the Israelites separated themselves from all foreigners and stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers. And they stood up in their place and read from the Book of the Law of the LORD their God for a quarter of the day; for another quarter of it they made confession and worshiped the LORD their God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now on the twenty-fourth day of this month the people of Israel were assembled with fasting and in sackcloth, and with earth on their heads. Two days after the last day of Booths. Three weeks earlier they had wept at the reading of the law and been told to stop, because it was a feast day (8:9-11). Now the feast is over, and the grief that was postponed is given its day.

Notice the order. God gave them the feast first and the fast second. They were told the joy of the LORD is your strength before they were told to put on sackcloth. People who already know God's delight in them can look at their sin without flinching and without despair. Confession that begins from terror usually stops short. Confession that begins from joy can go all the way down.

And the Israelites separated themselves from all foreigners and stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers. Not a rejection of any foreigner who had joined himself to the LORD (the Passover of Ezra 6:21 welcomed such), but a day on which Israel stood before God as Israel and owned its own history. Their sins and the iniquities of their fathers: they did not confess the present alone.

And they stood up in their place and read from the Book of the Law of the LORD their God for a quarter of the day; for another quarter of it they made confession and worshiped the LORD their God. Three hours of Scripture, then three hours of confession and worship. The reading came first, because a people cannot confess sins it has not been shown. The Word told them what to confess, and the worship told them to whom.

verseByVerse.quote: On the stairs of the Levites stood Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani; and they cried with a loud voice to the LORD their God. Then the Levites, Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabneiah, Sherebiah, Hodiah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, "Stand up and bless the LORD your God from everlasting to everlasting. Blessed be your glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the stairs of the Levites stood Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani; and they cried with a loud voice to the LORD their God. Several of these men had moved through the crowd three weeks before, helping the people understand the law (8:7). The teachers now lead the prayer. Understanding has become confession.

Stand up and bless the LORD your God from everlasting to everlasting. Blessed be your glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise.

They are in sackcloth, with dust on their heads, about to confess centuries of failure — and the first word is bless. Stand up and praise him. The confession will be addressed to a God whose name is higher than any praise they can give, and that is precisely what makes confession safe. You can tell the whole truth about yourself to a God like that.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–15 — You Are the LORD, You Alone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: You are the LORD, you alone: maker of heaven and earth and the seas, preserver of them all (v. 6); the God who chose Abram and made covenant with him to give his offspring the land — and you have kept your promise, for you are righteous (vv. 7-8). He saw Israel's affliction in Egypt, divided the sea, led them by cloud and fire (vv. 9-12), came down on Sinai and gave them good laws and his holy Sabbath (vv. 13-14), and fed them with bread from heaven and water from the rock (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Every verb in this part of the prayer has God for its subject. The history of Israel is told as the history of what God did.

verseByVerse.quote: "You are the LORD, you alone. You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their host, the earth and all that is on it, the seas and all that is in them; and you preserve all of them; and the host of heaven worships you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are the LORD, you alone. You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their host, the earth and all that is on it, the seas and all that is in them; and you preserve all of them; and the host of heaven worships you.

The prayer does not begin with Israel's trouble. It begins with the universe. Before a word about Persian taxes or broken covenants, they say who God is: the only one, maker of the highest heaven and the deepest sea, keeping every one of them in being moment by moment, and worshipped by the angels.

You alone was the confession their fathers had failed to make; it was the other gods that had sent them into exile. And it matters for everything that follows. If God is one of many, Israel's story is a contest between powers. If he alone made and holds all things, there has never been a moment in their history that was out of his hands, including the worst ones. The New Testament says who that Maker is: by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth ... all things were created through him and for him (Col 1:16).

verseByVerse.quote: You are the LORD, the God who chose Abram and brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans and gave him the name Abraham. You found his heart faithful before you, and made with him the covenant to give to his offspring the land of the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Jebusite, and the Girgashite. And you have kept your promise, for you are righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are the LORD, the God who chose Abram and brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans and gave him the name Abraham. From the whole creation to one man. God chose him, brought him out, and renamed him. Every verb is God's. And Ur of the Chaldeans is in Babylonia: the people praying had been brought out of the same country as their father Abraham.

You found his heart faithful before you, and made with him the covenant to give to his offspring the land of the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Jebusite, and the Girgashite. And you have kept your promise, for you are righteous.

You are righteous. Hold on to that phrase. Here it means that God kept his word: he promised the land and he gave it. In verse 33 it will come back — you have been righteous in all that has come upon us — and there it means that the exile was deserved. The prayer is bracketed by God's righteousness, once in the keeping of a promise and once in the carrying out of a sentence. He is the same God in both, and they trust him in both.

And look at the two words the verse puts together, faithful and righteous. Faithful is from the same Hebrew root as believed in the sentence the whole Bible turns on: he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness (Gen 15:6). God found in Abraham a heart that believed him, and counted it righteousness; and God himself turned out to be the righteous one, keeping every word. Paul builds the gospel on that verse (Rom 4:3). Abraham's faith was never the ground of the promise. God's righteousness was.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you saw the affliction of our fathers in Egypt and heard their cry at the Red Sea, and performed signs and wonders against Pharaoh and all his servants and all the people of his land, for you knew that they acted arrogantly against our fathers. And you made a name for yourself, as it is to this day. And you divided the sea before them, so that they went through the midst of the sea on dry land, and you cast their pursuers into the depths, as a stone into mighty waters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you saw the affliction of our fathers in Egypt and heard their cry at the Red Sea, and performed signs and wonders against Pharaoh. You saw ... and heard. The prayer remembers a God who noticed. For you knew that they acted arrogantly against our fathers. And you made a name for yourself, as it is to this day. The Exodus was not only a rescue; it was God making himself known, and the name he made there was still his name all those centuries later.

Mark that verb. They acted arrogantly is said of Egypt, and in verse 16 exactly the same Hebrew verb is said of Israel: they and our fathers acted presumptuously, and again in verse 29. The people God rescued from the arrogant became arrogant toward him. The prayer does not spare them the comparison. They had treated God the way Pharaoh had treated them.

And you divided the sea before them, so that they went through the midst of the sea on dry land, and you cast their pursuers into the depths, as a stone into mighty waters. The praying people knew what it was to be pursued by stronger nations. They remember the day God dropped the pursuers into the sea like a stone and the slaves walked through on dry ground.

verseByVerse.quote: By a pillar of cloud you led them in the day, and by a pillar of fire in the night to light for them the way in which they should go. You came down on Mount Sinai and spoke with them from heaven and gave them right rules and true laws, good statutes and commandments, and you made known to them your holy Sabbath and commanded them commandments and statutes and a law by Moses your servant. You gave them bread from heaven for their hunger and brought water for them out of the rock for their thirst, and you told them to go in to possess the land that you had sworn to give them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By a pillar of cloud you led them in the day, and by a pillar of fire in the night. Then Sinai: You came down on Mount Sinai and spoke with them from heaven and gave them right rules and true laws, good statutes and commandments. Right, true, good. The people confessing that they had broken the law begin by calling it good. The law was not their problem; they were.

And you made known to them your holy Sabbath. Of all the commandments, the Sabbath is the one named. It was a gift: a day of rest given to people who had been slaves and had never had one. It will matter again when Nehemiah finds the gates open for trade on that day (13:15-22).

You gave them bread from heaven for their hunger and brought water for them out of the rock for their thirst. Both of these, Jesus claimed for himself. My Father gives you the true bread from heaven ... I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst (John 6:32, 35). And Paul says of the rock: the Rock was Christ (1 Cor 10:4). The God who fed them in the desert was already giving them, in shadow, his Son.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–31 — You Did Not Forsake Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But they and our fathers acted presumptuously and stiffened their neck (v. 16), even choosing a leader to take them back to Egypt; but you are a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and did not forsake them (v. 17). Not after the golden calf (vv. 18-21); not through the conquest, when they grew fat on houses they had not built (vv. 22-25); not when they killed the prophets and he gave them into their enemies' hands and then sent saviors (vv. 26-28); not when they turned a stubborn shoulder for many years (vv. 29-30). Nevertheless, in your great mercies you did not make an end of them or forsake them, for you are a gracious and merciful God (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: Three times the prayer says God did not forsake them (vv. 17, 19, 31). Once, you abandoned them to the hand of their enemies (v. 28), the same verb. God gave them up for a time; he never gave them up for good.

verseByVerse.quote: "But they and our fathers acted presumptuously and stiffened their neck and did not obey your commandments. They refused to obey and were not mindful of the wonders that you performed among them, but they stiffened their neck and appointed a leader to return to their slavery in Egypt. But you are a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and did not forsake them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they and our fathers acted presumptuously and stiffened their neck and did not obey your commandments. They refused to obey and were not mindful of the wonders that you performed among them, but they stiffened their neck and appointed a leader to return to their slavery in Egypt.

Now the other side. Stiffened their neck, twice: the ox that will not bend to the yoke, as the nobles of Tekoa would not (3:5). And the worst of it: Let us choose a leader and go back to Egypt (Num 14:4). A people freed from slavery, fed daily from heaven, chose to go back to the brickworks rather than trust God for the land. Keep that in mind until verse 36, where the people praying say, we are slaves this day. Their fathers had asked to be slaves. They had been given what they asked for.

But you are a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and did not forsake them. This is the name God proclaimed to Moses on the mountain: The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exod 34:6). And he proclaimed it immediately after the golden calf, the worst sin in their history. God did not reveal his mercy to people who had deserved it. He revealed it to people who had just proved they did not. A God ready to forgive is, in Hebrew, a God of forgivenesses, plural: forgiveness, and more of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Even when they had made for themselves a golden calf and said, 'This is your God who brought you up out of Egypt,' and had committed great blasphemies, you in your great mercies did not forsake them in the wilderness. The pillar of cloud to lead them in the way did not depart from them by day, nor the pillar of fire by night to light for them the way by which they should go. You gave your good Spirit to instruct them and did not withhold your manna from their mouth and gave them water for their thirst. Forty years you sustained them in the wilderness, and they lacked nothing. Their clothes did not wear out and their feet did not swell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even when they had made for themselves a golden calf and said, This is your God who brought you up out of Egypt, and had committed great blasphemies, you in your great mercies did not forsake them in the wilderness. They credited a metal calf with the Exodus. And the very next thing the prayer records is that the pillar of cloud to lead them in the way did not depart from them by day, nor the pillar of fire by night. The morning after the calf, the cloud was still there. And the prayer describes it in almost the same words it used in verse 12, to light for them the way: nothing about God's leading had changed, though everything about their deserving had.

You gave your good Spirit to instruct them and did not withhold your manna from their mouth and gave them water for their thirst. Forty years you sustained them in the wilderness, and they lacked nothing. Their clothes did not wear out and their feet did not swell. Moses had said the same (Deut 8:4). Think of a single pair of sandals, walked in for forty years, and never worn through. That is the care of God for people in the middle of their rebellion. And first in the list is not food but your good Spirit to instruct them. God did not only feed rebels; he went on teaching them. The same Spirit is promised to believers now, to teach you all things (John 14:26).

Many readers know what it is to have wandered in some wilderness of their own making and to look back and see that God fed them the whole way. Their sandals did not wear out either. That is not a reason to presume on him. It is a reason to come home.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you gave them kingdoms and peoples and allotted to them every corner. So they took possession of the land of Sihon king of Heshbon and the land of Og king of Bashan. You multiplied their children as the stars of heaven, and you brought them into the land that you had told their fathers to enter and possess. So the descendants went in and possessed the land, and you subdued before them the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, and gave them into their hand, with their kings and the peoples of the land, that they might do with them as they would. And they captured fortified cities and a rich land, and took possession of houses full of all good things, cisterns already hewn, vineyards, olive orchards and fruit trees in abundance. So they ate and were filled and became fat and delighted themselves in your great goodness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the land. Kingdoms given, Sihon and Og defeated, children multiplied as the stars of heaven, and the Canaanites handed over (vv. 22-24). The stars go back to the night God took Abraham outside and said, number the stars, if you are able to number them ... So shall your offspring be (Gen 15:5). Verse 8 said he kept his promise; verse 23 shows it kept. And they captured fortified cities and a rich land, and took possession of houses full of all good things, cisterns already hewn, vineyards, olive orchards and fruit trees in abundance.

That is almost word for word what Moses had promised, and warned: houses full of all good things that you did not fill, and cisterns that you did not dig, and vineyards and olive trees that you did not plant — and when you eat and are full, then take care lest you forget the LORD (Deut 6:11-12).

So they ate and were filled and became fat and delighted themselves in your great goodness. Delighted themselves in his goodness. There is nothing wrong in that sentence; it is what the gifts were for. But Moses had also sung what would happen next: Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked ... then he forsook God who made him (Deut 32:15). The danger of blessing is that we come to love the house and forget who filled it. A test we can run on ourselves: when life is full, do we pray more, or less?

verseByVerse.quote: "Nevertheless, they were disobedient and rebelled against you and cast your law behind their back and killed your prophets, who had warned them in order to turn them back to you, and they committed great blasphemies. Therefore you gave them into the hand of their enemies, who made them suffer. And in the time of their suffering they cried out to you and you heard them from heaven, and according to your great mercies you gave them saviors who saved them from the hand of their enemies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nevertheless, they were disobedient and rebelled against you and cast your law behind their back and killed your prophets, who had warned them in order to turn them back to you, and they committed great blasphemies.

Cast your law behind their back: not lost, not forgotten, but thrown over the shoulder so that they would not have to look at it. And killed your prophets. Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned to death in the temple court for delivering God's message (2 Chr 24:20-21). Jesus wept over the same city for the same reason: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! (Luke 13:34). And then they killed him too.

Therefore you gave them into the hand of their enemies, who made them suffer. And in the time of their suffering they cried out to you and you heard them from heaven, and according to your great mercies you gave them saviors who saved them from the hand of their enemies. That is the book of Judges in one sentence: the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, the LORD raised up a deliverer ... who saved them (Judg 3:9). One savior after another, each for a generation. They were waiting, without knowing it, for the announcement to the shepherds: unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord (Luke 2:11).

verseByVerse.quote: But after they had rest they did evil again before you, and you abandoned them to the hand of their enemies, so that they had dominion over them. Yet when they turned and cried to you, you heard from heaven, and many times you delivered them according to your mercies. And you warned them in order to turn them back to your law. Yet they acted presumptuously and did not obey your commandments, but sinned against your rules, which if a person does them, he shall live by them, and they turned a stubborn shoulder and stiffened their neck and would not obey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But after they had rest they did evil again before you, and you abandoned them to the hand of their enemies, so that they had dominion over them. Yet when they turned and cried to you, you heard from heaven, and many times you delivered them according to your mercies.

After they had rest they did evil again. Not in hardship but in rest; it was the good years that undid them. And notice the word abandoned. It is the same Hebrew verb as did not forsake in verses 17, 19 and 31. The prayer is honest: God did give them up to their enemies, for a time. What he never did was give them up for good. Many times you delivered them. Many times. Mercy that could be counted would have run out long before.

And you warned them in order to turn them back to your law. Yet they acted presumptuously and did not obey your commandments, but sinned against your rules, which if a person does them, he shall live by them. That clause is Leviticus 18:5, and it is the law's own promise: do this and live. They did not do it, and neither has anyone else. Paul quotes the same verse — The one who does them shall live by them — and then says what God did about it: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Gal 3:12-13). The one Man who did them, and could have lived by them, died under the curse that belonged to those who did not.

verseByVerse.quote: Many years you bore with them and warned them by your Spirit through your prophets. Yet they would not give ear. Therefore you gave them into the hand of the peoples of the lands. Nevertheless, in your great mercies you did not make an end of them or forsake them, for you are a gracious and merciful God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many years you bore with them and warned them by your Spirit through your prophets. Yet they would not give ear. Many years: the prophets spoke for centuries, from Elijah to Jeremiah. The picture in verse 29, that they turned a stubborn shoulder and stiffened their neck, is an ox shrugging off the yoke, and Zechariah had used the same words of their fathers (Zech 7:11). He had also said whose voice they were refusing: the words that the LORD of hosts had sent by his Spirit through the former prophets (Zech 7:12). The prophets' words were the Spirit's words. They were refusing God, not men. Therefore you gave them into the hand of the peoples of the lands: the exile.

Nevertheless, in your great mercies you did not make an end of them or forsake them, for you are a gracious and merciful God.

That nevertheless is the hinge of the whole history. The exile was deserved, and it was not the end. They were standing in Jerusalem saying so. Ezra had prayed the same: for we are slaves. Yet our God has not forsaken us in our slavery (Ezra 9:9).

And the reason God could promise never to forsake people who had forsaken him for centuries is that one day he would forsake someone else in their place. At the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice ... My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Mark 15:34). He was abandoned so that his people would hear, and keep hearing, I will never leave you nor forsake you (Heb 13:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–38 — Behold, We Are Slaves This Day
