verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now, therefore, our God, the great, the mighty, and the awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love, let not all the hardship seem little to you (v. 32). Yet you have been righteous in all that has come upon us, for you have dealt faithfully and we have acted wickedly (v. 33). Their kings and priests and fathers would not serve him in their own rich land (vv. 34-35); behold, we are slaves this day, and the harvest goes to the kings set over them because of their sins (vv. 36-37). Because of all this we make a firm covenant in writing (v. 38).
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer asks for one thing, that God would not think their hardship small, and it asks it while agreeing that every blow was deserved. It is the confession of people who know their only hope is the character of the God they have wronged.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now, therefore, our God, the great, the mighty, and the awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love, let not all the hardship seem little to you that has come upon us, upon our kings, our princes, our priests, our prophets, our fathers, and all your people, since the time of the kings of Assyria until this day. Yet you have been righteous in all that has come upon us, for you have dealt faithfully and we have acted wickedly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now, therefore, our God, the great, the mighty, and the awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love, let not all the hardship seem little to you that has come upon us, upon our kings, our princes, our priests, our prophets, our fathers, and all your people, since the time of the kings of Assyria until this day.

The history has reached the present, and the prayer turns to God with the words of Moses — the great, the mighty, and the awesome God (Deut 10:17) — and of Nehemiah's own first prayer (1:5). And the one request in the entire prayer is modest: do not let our hardship look small to you. Since the time of the kings of Assyria: three centuries of invasion, deportation, siege and subjection, from Assyria to Babylon to Persia. Look at it, Lord. Do not treat it as nothing.

Yet you have been righteous in all that has come upon us, for you have dealt faithfully and we have acted wickedly. And in the same breath: it was all just. That is the heart of true confession. They ask God to see their suffering, and they agree with every stroke of it. You have been faithful; we have been wicked. No excuses, no blaming the kings of Assyria. The man who can pray verse 33 without an exception has been brought to the place where mercy can reach him.

verseByVerse.quote: Our kings, our princes, our priests, and our fathers have not kept your law or paid attention to your commandments and your warnings that you gave them. Even in their own kingdom, and amid your great goodness that you gave them, and in the large and rich land that you set before them, they did not serve you or turn from their wicked works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our kings, our princes, our priests, and our fathers have not kept your law or paid attention to your commandments and your warnings that you gave them. Every rank is named; nobody is left outside the confession.

With one exception. In verse 32 the hardship fell on our kings, our princes, our priests, our prophets, our fathers. In verse 34 the ones who did not keep the law are our kings, our princes, our priests, and our fathers. The prophets have dropped out of the list. They suffered with the nation, went into exile with it (Jeremiah to Egypt, Ezekiel and Daniel to Babylon), and were not the cause of it. The innocent went down with the guilty. One Prophet went further, and suffered not only with the guilty but for them.

Even in their own kingdom, and amid your great goodness that you gave them, and in the large and rich land that you set before them, they did not serve you or turn from their wicked works. Their own kingdom: they had had a king of their own, a land of their own, and every good thing in it, and they did not serve you. Hold that verb. It is about to come back.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, we are slaves this day; in the land that you gave to our fathers to enjoy its fruit and its good gifts, behold, we are slaves. And its rich yield goes to the kings whom you have set over us because of our sins. They rule over our bodies and over our livestock as they please, and we are in great distress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, we are slaves this day; in the land that you gave to our fathers to enjoy its fruit and its good gifts, behold, we are slaves.

Slaves and serve are the same word in Hebrew. They would not serve God in their own kingdom (v. 35), and so they serve as slaves in their own land. God had said exactly this to Rehoboam's generation: they shall be servants to him, that they may know my service and the service of the kingdoms of the countries (2 Chr 12:8). Every people serves someone. Refuse the service of God and you do not become free; you learn the service of the kingdoms. And the fathers who had once asked for a leader to take them back to slavery (v. 17) had got their wish.

And its rich yield goes to the kings whom you have set over us because of our sins. They rule over our bodies and over our livestock as they please, and we are in great distress. The Persian king who sent Nehemiah had been generous to him, but the harvest of Judah still went east in tribute, and the empire could conscript their bodies and their animals. Whom you have set over us: even the empire is God's doing. We are in great distress. The prayer ends there.

There is only one way out of that kind of slavery, and it is not a better master in Persia. If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:36).

verseByVerse.quote: "Because of all this we make a firm covenant in writing; on the sealed document are the names of our princes, our Levites, and our priests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because of all this we make a firm covenant in writing; on the sealed document are the names of our princes, our Levites, and our priests.

Because of all this — the whole history, the mercy and the rebellion, the slavery they are in. They do not answer with a feeling but with a document. They will put it in writing, seal it, and sign their names, so that there can be no quiet forgetting later. The next chapter is the list of those who signed and what they promised.

It is right to bind oneself to God in this way, and chapter 13 will show how quickly the promises of chapter 10 were broken. A covenant with our names on it cannot save us. What saves is the covenant with God's name on it, the new covenant in my blood (Luke 22:20), sealed by the one party who has never failed to keep his word.

9.theology:
The whole history is told with God as its subject. God is righteous in keeping his promise (v. 8) and righteous in the judgment (v. 33), and between those two verses his people rebel again and again and he does not forsake them. Mercy that could be counted would have run out.

The prayer lives on shadows that Christ fills: the bread from heaven and the rock (John 6:35; 1 Cor 10:4), the saviors of the judges (Luke 2:11), the prophets Jerusalem killed (Luke 13:34), the law that promises life to the one who does it (Lev 18:5), which he did and whose curse he bore (Gal 3:12-13). God could promise never to forsake a people who had forsaken him because he would forsake his Son in their place (Mark 15:34; Heb 13:5).
9.examples:
The fast came after the feast.

They read Scripture for three hours before they confessed for three.

In sackcloth, the first word was bless.

The morning after the golden calf, the cloud was still there.

Forty years in the same sandals.

Their fathers asked for a leader back to slavery; the children say we are slaves this day.

They would not serve God, so they served Persia.

The one request: do not let our hardship seem small to you.

10.overview: The sealed covenant of 9:38 bears eighty-four names: Nehemiah the governor first, with Zedekiah, then twenty-one priests, seventeen Levites and forty-four chiefs of the people, most of them the family names of the first return (vv. 1-27). The rest of the people, with their wives and children and every convert who had separated himself to the Law of God, join them under a curse and an oath to walk in God's law (vv. 28-29). The terms are specific: no marriages with the peoples of the land (v. 30); no buying on the Sabbath; the seventh year kept and debts released (v. 31); a yearly third of a shekel for the temple's offerings (vv. 32-33); the wood for the altar brought by lot (v. 34); firstfruits, firstborn and tithes brought to the priests and Levites (vv. 35-39). It ends: We will not neglect the house of our God (v. 39) — a promise chapter 13 will find broken.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–27 — On the Seals Are the Names
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the seals are the names of Nehemiah the governor, the son of Hacaliah, Zedekiah (v. 1), then twenty-one priests (vv. 2-8), seventeen Levites (vv. 9-13), and forty-four chiefs of the people (vv. 14-27) — eighty-four names on the sealed document of 9:38.
verseByVerse.theology: They put their names to it. A covenant with names on it cannot be quietly forgotten later, and that is exactly why they wanted one. The same names turn up in the next chapters, some keeping the promise and some breaking it.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the seals are the names of Nehemiah the governor, the son of Hacaliah, Zedekiah,
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the seals are the names of Nehemiah the governor, the son of Hacaliah, Zedekiah. The prayer of chapter 9 ended with a firm covenant in writing and the sealed document (9:38). This is its signature page. A seal pressed into clay or wax was a man's signature in that world: it said, this is mine, and I stand behind it.

The first name is the governor's. Nehemiah did not ask the people to bind themselves to anything he had not bound himself to first. It is the same man who stopped the moneylenders by saying let us abandon this exacting of interest (5:10), including himself. Zedekiah, next to him, was probably his secretary.

verseByVerse.quote: Seraiah, Azariah, Jeremiah, Pashhur, Amariah, Malchijah, Hattush, Shebaniah, Malluch, Harim, Meremoth, Obadiah, Daniel, Ginnethon, Baruch, Meshullam, Abijah, Mijamin, Maaziah, Bilgai, Shemaiah; these are the priests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twenty-one priests: Seraiah, Azariah, Jeremiah and the rest. Most of these are the names of priestly houses rather than individuals; many of them reappear in the list of priestly families in 12:1-21. A family signs through its head.

Two names stand out. Meremoth (v. 5) recalls the priest of the family of Hakkoz who built two sections of the wall (3:4, 21), from a family once barred from the priesthood for want of a genealogy (7:63-64). And Abijah (v. 7) is a priestly house that will be heard of again. When David divided the priests into twenty-four divisions, the lots fell the seventh to Hakkoz, the eighth to Abijah (1 Chr 24:10). Five centuries after Nehemiah, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah (Luke 1:5), and while he was serving his turn in the temple an angel told him he would have a son, who would prepare the way for the Lord. The name on this seal is the name of the division in which John the Baptist's father served.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Levites: Jeshua the son of Azaniah, Binnui of the sons of Henadad, Kadmiel; and their brothers, Shebaniah, Hodiah, Kelita, Pelaiah, Hanan, Mica, Rehob, Hashabiah, Zaccur, Sherebiah, Shebaniah, Hodiah, Bani, Beninu.
verseByVerse.commentary: Seventeen Levites. Jeshua ... Binnui ... Kadmiel, and among them Shebaniah, Hodiah, Kelita, Pelaiah, Hanan, Sherebiah and Bani. Several of these are the men who explained the law to the crowd at the Water Gate (8:7) and led the confession from the stairs (9:4-5). They taught it, they prayed it, and now they sign it. The teachers put their own names under the obligations they had been explaining to everyone else.

verseByVerse.quote: The chiefs of the people: Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam, Zattu, Bani, Bunni, Azgad, Bebai, Adonijah, Bigvai, Adin, Ater, Hezekiah, Azzur, Hodiah, Hashum, Bezai, Hariph, Anathoth, Nebai, Magpiash, Meshullam, Hezir, Meshezabel, Zadok, Jaddua, Pelatiah, Hanan, Anaiah, Hoshea, Hananiah, Hasshub, Hallohesh, Pilha, Shobek, Rehum, Hashabnah, Maaseiah, Ahiah, Hanan, Anan, Malluch, Harim, Baanah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chiefs of the people: Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam, Zattu, Bani — forty-four of them. Read them against the register in chapter 7 and most are old friends: Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam, Zattu, Azgad, Bebai, Bigvai, Adin, Ater, Hashum, Bezai, Hariph, even Anathoth, which is a town. These are the family names of those who came home ninety years before, now signing through their present heads. The children of the first return were renewing their fathers' covenant.

And a few names from the wall. Hallohesh (v. 24) is the family of Shallum, who built his section he and his daughters (3:12). Hasshub (v. 23) built opposite his own house (3:23). There is a Meshullam here too (v. 20), a common name, and the reader remembers another Meshullam who built two sections and then married his daughter to Tobiah's son (6:18). Names on a covenant are only as good as the hearts behind them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–31 — To Walk in God's Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rest of the people join them — priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, temple servants, all who have separated themselves from the peoples of the lands to the Law of God, with their wives and children — under a curse and an oath to walk in God's Law (vv. 28-29). They will not give their children in marriage to the peoples of the land (v. 30); they will not buy on the Sabbath; and we will forgo the crops of the seventh year and the exaction of every debt (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: The covenant addresses the three places where the community had actually been failing: its marriages, its Sabbaths and its debts. It is specific because their disobedience had been specific.

verseByVerse.quote: "The rest of the people, the priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, the singers, the temple servants, and all who have separated themselves from the peoples of the lands to the Law of God, their wives, their sons, their daughters, all who have knowledge and understanding, join with their brothers, their nobles, and enter into a curse and an oath to walk in God's Law that was given by Moses the servant of God, and to observe and do all the commandments of the LORD our Lord and his rules and his statutes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rest of the people, the priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, the singers, the temple servants, and all who have separated themselves from the peoples of the lands to the Law of God, their wives, their sons, their daughters, all who have knowledge and understanding, join with their brothers, their nobles, and enter into a curse and an oath to walk in God's Law.

Everyone who could understand, as at the reading (8:2), wives and daughters included. And notice how belonging is defined: those who separated themselves from the peoples of the lands to the Law of God. The separation is toward something. A foreigner who turned from his gods to the law of the LORD was inside this sentence, as such people had been at the Passover ninety years before (Ezra 6:21). The line runs round a way of worship, not round a bloodline.

And they join with their brothers, their nobles. Not long before, the people had raised a great outcry ... against their Jewish brothers, the nobles who held their fields and their daughters (5:1-5). Now the same people stand beside the same nobles under one oath. The debts had been returned, and the brothers were brothers again. Reconciliation came before the covenant, not after it.

A curse and an oath: they swore, and called down on themselves the curses of the law if they broke it. That is a serious thing to do, and they meant it. Chapter 13 will show how much it was worth in practice. It is also the reason we need a better covenant than one we can sign ourselves.

verseByVerse.quote: We will not give our daughters to the peoples of the land or take their daughters for our sons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We will not give our daughters to the peoples of the land or take their daughters for our sons.

This is Deuteronomy 7:3, and the law gave its reason in the next verse: they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods (Deut 7:4). The concern is the worship of the home, not the blood of the partner, which is why the proselyte is included in verse 28. Nehemiah will find the promise broken within a few years, with children who could not speak the language of Judah (13:23-24).

A Christian reader will want to know how this applies now, and the New Testament answers both halves plainly. To the unmarried: marry only in the Lord (1 Cor 7:39). To the believer who is already married to an unbeliever: he should not divorce her, and she should not divorce him, for the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife (1 Cor 7:12-14). The promise of this verse is about marriages not yet made. It gives no one a warrant to leave a marriage that already exists.

verseByVerse.quote: And if the peoples of the land bring in goods or any grain on the Sabbath day to sell, we will not buy from them on the Sabbath or on a holy day. And we will forgo the crops of the seventh year and the exaction of every debt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And if the peoples of the land bring in goods or any grain on the Sabbath day to sell, we will not buy from them on the Sabbath or on a holy day. The Sabbath law forbade Israel to work; it did not stop foreign traders from setting up stalls. The covenant closes the gap: if we cannot sell, we will not buy either. It is exactly this gap that Nehemiah finds wide open in 13:15-16, with the men of Tyre selling fish in Jerusalem on the Sabbath.

And we will forgo the crops of the seventh year and the exaction of every debt. Every seventh year the land was to lie fallow, that the poor of your people may eat (Exod 23:11), and debts between Israelites were to be released: every creditor shall release what he has lent to his neighbor. He shall not exact it of his neighbor, his brother (Deut 15:2). That is chapter 5 written into law. The fathers who had sold their daughters for debt (5:5) now have it in writing, sealed by the nobles, that debts will not be allowed to grind a family down for ever.

A test for a Christian's week: is there anything in the way we buy, sell and lend that says we belong to a God who gives rest and forgives debts? The Sabbath and the seventh year were God's people saying with their calendars and their account books that they trusted him to provide.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–39 — We Will Not Neglect the House of Our God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They bind themselves to pay a yearly third of a shekel for the temple's offerings (vv. 32-33), to take turns bringing wood for the altar (v. 34), and to bring firstfruits, firstborn, the first of the dough, and tithes to the priests and Levites, with the Levites bringing a tenth of the tithe to the storehouse (vv. 35-39). We will not neglect the house of our God (v. 39).
verseByVerse.theology: Neglect is the verb that meant forsake in the prayer of chapter 9: God did not forsake them. Now they promise not to forsake his house. In chapter 13 Nehemiah will come back and ask, Why is the house of God forsaken? (13:11).

verseByVerse.quote: "We also take on ourselves the obligation to give yearly a third part of a shekel for the service of the house of our God: for the showbread, the regular grain offering, the regular burnt offering, the Sabbaths, the new moons, the appointed feasts, the holy things, and the sin offerings to make atonement for Israel, and for all the work of the house of our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We also take on ourselves the obligation to give yearly a third part of a shekel for the service of the house of our God: for the showbread, the regular grain offering, the regular burnt offering, the Sabbaths, the new moons, the appointed feasts, the holy things, and the sin offerings to make atonement for Israel, and for all the work of the house of our God.

The law had set a half shekel for each man counted in Israel, the same for everyone: the rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less ... to make atonement for your lives (Exod 30:15). The community, poor and in debt, pledges a third, and pledges it every year. By Jesus' day the temple tax was back at the half shekel, and the collectors asked Peter whether his teacher paid it. Jesus asked whether kings tax their own sons, and said, Then the sons are free. The Son owed nothing to his Father's house. He paid it anyway, with a coin from a fish's mouth: give it to them for me and for yourself (Matt 17:26-27). One coin, for the Son and for the disciple together.

And see what the tax paid for, year after year: the sin offerings to make atonement for Israel. The offerings never stopped because the sins never stopped. Every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down (Heb 10:11-12). The yearly third of a shekel was a standing order for atonement. It was cancelled when the account was paid in full.

verseByVerse.quote: We, the priests, the Levites, and the people, have likewise cast lots for the wood offering, to bring it into the house of our God, according to our fathers' houses, at times appointed, year by year, to burn on the altar of the LORD our God, as it is written in the Law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We, the priests, the Levites, and the people, have likewise cast lots for the wood offering, to bring it into the house of our God, according to our fathers' houses, at times appointed, year by year, to burn on the altar of the LORD our God, as it is written in the Law.

There is no law in the Pentateuch setting up a rota for firewood. What is written is this: The fire on the altar shall be kept burning on it; it shall not go out. The priest shall burn wood on it every morning (Lev 6:12). If the fire must never go out, somebody must bring the wood. On the hills round Jerusalem, where the trees had been cut for a century and a half, that meant organized families taking turns, by lot, year after year. This is what obedience looks like when it takes a command seriously enough to work out the practical cost.

It is also the last thing Nehemiah mentions in his whole book: and I provided for the wood offering at appointed times (13:31). The final entry in a great man's record is the firewood.

verseByVerse.quote: We obligate ourselves to bring the firstfruits of our ground and the firstfruits of all fruit of every tree, year by year, to the house of the LORD; also to bring to the house of our God, to the priests who minister in the house of our God, the firstborn of our sons and of our cattle, as it is written in the Law, and the firstborn of our herds and of our flocks; and to bring the first of our dough, and our contributions, the fruit of every tree, the wine and the oil, to the priests, to the chambers of the house of our God; and to bring to the Levites the tithes from our ground, for it is the Levites who collect the tithes in all our towns where we labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the firsts: the firstfruits of our ground and the firstfruits of all fruit of every tree, the firstborn of our sons and of our cattle, the first of our dough. Each is a law of Moses (Exod 23:19; 13:13; Num 15:20). The first of everything went to God, before the family ate or sold any of it. The firstborn sons were not sacrificed but redeemed with a price, a reminder that every family in Israel owed its eldest to the God who spared them on the night of the Passover.

And the tithes, a tenth of the harvest, go to the Levites, for it is the Levites who collect the tithes in all our towns where we labor. The Levites had no land of their own; they lived on what God's people gave. If the tithes stopped, the Levites went back to the fields to feed their families, and the temple service stopped with them. That is exactly what Nehemiah will find: the Levites and the singers, who did the work, had fled each to his field (13:10).

verseByVerse.quote: And the priest, the son of Aaron, shall be with the Levites when the Levites receive the tithes. And the Levites shall bring up the tithe of the tithes to the house of our God, to the chambers of the storehouse. For the people of Israel and the sons of Levi shall bring the contribution of grain, wine, and oil to the chambers, where the vessels of the sanctuary are, as well as the priests who minister, and the gatekeepers and the singers. We will not neglect the house of our God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the priest, the son of Aaron, shall be with the Levites when the Levites receive the tithes. And the Levites shall bring up the tithe of the tithes to the house of our God, to the chambers of the storehouse. A priest present at every collection, so that the counting is witnessed; and the Levites give a tenth of what they receive (Num 18:26). Nobody in the system is exempt from giving, not even the people who live on the gifts.

Notice how often the chambers are mentioned: the chambers of the house of our God (v. 37), the chambers of the storehouse (v. 38), the chambers, where the vessels of the sanctuary are (v. 39). These storerooms in the temple courts were where the grain, wine and oil for the Levites were kept. Remember them. When Nehemiah comes back in chapter 13 he finds that Eliashib the priest has emptied a large chamber where they had previously put the grain offering, the frankincense, the vessels, and the tithes of grain, wine, and oil and moved Tobiah the Ammonite into it, furniture and all (13:4-5).

For the people of Israel and the sons of Levi shall bring the contribution of grain, wine, and oil to the chambers ... We will not neglect the house of our God.

The last line is the summary of the whole covenant, and its verb carries the weight of the whole book. Neglect is the Hebrew word translated forsake in the great prayer: you ... did not forsake them (9:19). God had not forsaken them through nine centuries of rebellion. They answer: then we will not forsake your house. Years later Nehemiah will stand in the temple and ask, with the same word, Why is the house of God forsaken? (13:11).

That is not a reason to despise their promise. It was right and good. It is a reason to see why a covenant signed by us, however sincerely, is not enough. The new covenant is the one in which God makes the promises and keeps both sides: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jer 31:33). The house of God is safe at last in the hands of the Son, of whom it was written, Zeal for your house will consume me (John 2:17).

10.theology:
After hearing the law and confessing their history, the people bind themselves in writing to specific obedience in the very places they had failed: marriage, Sabbath, debt, and the support of God's house. It is right that God's people make such commitments, and chapter 13 shows why such commitments cannot save them.

The yearly tax paid for sin offerings that never ended until Christ offered one sacrifice for all time (Heb 10:11-12). The Son who owed no tax to his Father's house paid it for himself and his disciple (Matt 17:26-27), and the new covenant is the one God keeps from both sides (Jer 31:33).
10.examples:
The governor signed first.

The priestly house of Abijah set its seal here; John the Baptist's father was of that division.

The Levites who taught the law and led the confession signed it too.

The debt reform of chapter 5 was written into the covenant.

They worked out a firewood rota because the fire on the altar must never go out.

Even the Levites gave a tenth of what they received.

We will not neglect — the verb of did not forsake them in the prayer.
